entry.title: America Finally Has the Good Sunscreen
entry.summary: The sunscreen filter, which is finally Stateside after many years in Europe and Asia, offers broad UV protection and a lightweight feel.
entry.content:
A few weeks ago, a package from Neutrogena turned up on my doorstep. It featured their latest release of sunscreens and unlike launches past, which contain the same chemical filters I’ve been seeing for a decade with riffs on feel and invisibility, this one had a new filter, bemotrizinol, the first new sunscreen filter approved by the FDA in 27 years. As I wrote about shortly after the announcement, bemotrizinol is a broad-spectrum filter, which protects against both UVA and UVB rays. Most do one or the other. It’s also a bit more stable and degrades slower than the chemical filters we’re used to. That means the time advertised on the bottle is a bit more accurate, so you can be confident about the level of protection you receive. Originally, the ingredient was limited to a single manufacturer, but we’ve seen it popping up in multiple formulas over the past few months.

This is the sunscreen I’ve been testing. It’s reminiscent of the K Beauty sunscreens I’ve tried in that it’s lightweight and nongreasy but still moisturizing. It contains micro-peptide technology to support collagen production and a high SPF factor of 70, protecting against at least 98 percent of UV rays. Another bonus is that it contains antioxidants, which helps to guard against oxidative stress and hyperpigmentation.

There’s also an acne-prone skin version, which is noncomedogenic and has ingredients that help with hyperpigmentation like vitamin E and niacinamide. It’s slightly thinner than the Ultra Sheer formula and sinks in quickly, ideal for wearing under makeup.

Another ultra-lightweight option, this one goes on and disappears near-instantly. It’s packed with antioxidants, including Exo-P, a ferment extract that protects skin from smog and pollution.

entry.title: The 3 Very Best Robot Vacuums for Pets
entry.summary: Hands-off options for staying on top of pet hair.
entry.content:
Last year, my household went from having two small dogs who hardly shed to five dogs. Between the dirt they track in after going outside, the fur the larger three shed, and the occasional turf war that leaves my floors covered in pee, things easily get out of hand. Without a robot vacuum, I’d probably spend half my nights sweeping and scrubbing my floors.

If you have pets, even if your situation isn’t as extreme as mine, you’ll probably find that having a robot vacuum will cut down on the amount of time and effort you spend cleaning up after them. But when it comes to pet messes on your floors, some models are more effective than others. For carpets or rugs, you’ll want a robot vacuum with a good brush that can avoid tangles plus enough suction power to pick up dirt and hair that’s embedded in your carpet or rug’s fibers. But if you have hardwood or tile floors, your pets likely drag dirt and other nasty stuff all across them, so a robot with a mop function might be the way to go.

I’ve tested more than 20 robot vacuums since I started covering them in 2023, including several with mopping capabilities. Because I’ve never not had at least two dogs living with me, every model we’ve recommended has proved to be up to the task of handling a household with pets. In addition, I ran each robot vacuum over my floors at least three times to see how effectively each one avoids random obstacles, such as toys and cables, that your pets may not always leave in the same place. And since none of the five dogs in my home have particularly long fur, I had each vacuum run over some long hairs from a wig and noted whether any tangles resulted and if the vacuum was able to eliminate them. Plus, because pets can be sensitive to noise and it’s often best to run these robots when they aren’t in the room, I also tried out each vacuum’s smart scheduling and single-room cleaning.

Updated on October 30, 2026
I’ve added the Narwal Flow 2 as the new best robot vacuum-mop combo for pets. Everything else is still available and the prices are up to date.

If you have a dog or cat that sheds, it’s important that your robot vacuum’s brushes don’t get stalled by tangled hair (and this is even more important if you have a long-haired pet or household member). Some robot vacs use single brushes, while others have a dual-brush system that digs deep into rug fibers to yank out tough-to-clean gunk. I’ve also seen newer models with single brushes that are split into two parts to better avoid tangles, as well as some with blades that can cut through clumps of pet hair.

Quality brushes don’t just make for a more thorough cleaning; the better the brushes are at sweeping up debris that rests below the surface of a rug or carpet or in crevices, the less suction power the vacuum will have to use. That trade-off can save a lot of battery life, as a vacuum that’s always running at max suction will have to return to the docking station to recharge more frequently, resulting in longer overall cleaning times.

While this wasn’t a huge consideration a few years ago, robot vacuums have significantly more powerful suction now. They still can’t match the suction power of upright or cordless stick vacuums, but they finally have enough power to pick up things that can get stuck deep in the fibers of a rug or carpet — like pet hair. Suction power on robot vacuums is typically measured in pascals (pa) to indicate how much air pressure is being applied. The higher the pa, the more suction power your vacuum’s going to provide.

If you have cats or dogs, there’s a good chance your vacuum will pick up a lot — we mean a lot — of dirt, hair, and other particles. Vacuums with large, self-emptying base stations can hold more dirt than the on-device dustbin, meaning you don’t spend as much time cleaning your robot, and your robot can periodically empty itself throughout a cleaning job to make sure it gets the whole house clean and to keep things running smoothly. You can get models without these base stations for less money, but you’ll have to empty them manually — and frequently.

Run time on a robot vacuum isn’t quite as important as it is with other kinds of vacuums, since a robot has more time to get its cleaning done than you do and it can return to base for a recharge. That said, the longer its run time, the less frequently it’ll have to stop its cleaning job to return to the dock and recharge, meaning you’re more likely to come home to a clean house. Some robots can calculate how much battery they’ll need to finish a cleaning job and only recharge to that percentage, rather than spending more time doing a full recharge. Others will wait to hit 100 percent before resuming cleaning.

Newer vacuums use lasers or cameras to map the layout of your home to avoid obstacles far better than older robots that relied on bumping into things to figure out where they were going. Those that use lasers won’t pick up as many details as those with cameras, as they can’t use object/obstacle detection to avoid things that tend to move around the house unpredictably, like dog or cat toys, bowls, and, in some cases, poop.

On the other hand, laser-based robots without cameras pose fewer privacy risks. They may still save some data about your home, like a blueprint of its layout, but they won’t take any pictures that could contain sensitive information. That doesn’t mean companies don’t work to ensure that their camera-based robots protect your data and your privacy — they do — but if you’re the type to keep a smart speaker out of your home so nobody’s listening, you’re better off with a laser-only robot or one without mapping capabilities.

While companies don’t always publish a lot of details about their filtration systems, we only recommend those with HEPA filters for helping to remove dust, pollen, and pet dander from the air. Those without HEPA filters will simply recirculate those particles around your room and won’t provide as much relief for those with allergies as vacuums with HEPA filters.

Not every home needs a robot with a built-in mop, but they’re worth considering if you have multiple pets. They won’t scrub your floors quite as well as doing it manually (or as well as a dedicated robot mop), but the best robots get about 80 percent of the way there. Most of these robots have two circular pads that are raised until the mopping function is activated so they don’t come into contact with carpets or rugs. They also typically have a self-cleaning function built into their docks that will routinely clean the mopping pads throughout a cleaning job to ensure it isn’t just spreading dirty water across the floor.

Every parent I’ve spoken to about robot vacuums has asked if there are any models with a child lock. Most manufacturers allow you to toggle this mode from the robot’s app.

Brushes: Single-brush system | Suction power: 10,000 pa | Disposal: Self-emptying base station | Run time: 150 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors | Filtration: Yes | Mopping: Yes | Child lock: Yes

Roborock’s Q7 M5+ has enough suction power to pick up clumps of dog or cat hair, the ability to mop, and some of the best smart navigation I’ve seen in a robot. Even with all the bowls, toys, and random items my dogs leave on the floors, it’s managed to avoid nearly every obstacle in its path as well as robots more than double its price, all while leaving my floors notably cleaner.

That’s mostly thanks to Roborock’s intelligent software. It mapped my home in just under half an hour, while other robots took up to 15 minutes longer. Once that’s set up, you can have it run an automatic cleaning job with stock settings or fine-tune things like how much suction the robot’s using, the intensity of the mopping function, and how many times it goes over your floors. You can also schedule cleaning routines, set times where the robot can’t run at all, and put it in child-lock mode so kids can’t turn it on at will.

If your pets tend to spend a lot of time in a particular area — near their bed, food bowls, or play area — you can set custom zones to have the robot target those areas without doing a full cycle through your home. There’s also an option to create no-go zones to avoid any areas where it might get caught up, like near a power strip.

In addition to vacuuming, the Q7 also has a mopping function that’s been good enough to keep my floors tidy despite the constant dirt my dogs track in. Unlike other mopping robots we recommend, however, this one uses a single, non-rotating pad that it pushes down to scrub your floors. It can’t apply as much pressure as robots like the Narwal Flow 2 that have more powerful mops, so it’s not as effective for scrubbing out sticky messes. Additionally, the docking station doesn’t have a cleaning function for the mopping pad, so you’ll have to remove the pad and either clean it by hand or toss it in the washing machine. If you find yourself needing to mop regularly, Narwal’s Flow 2 is worth the extra money.

Brushes: Single brush | Suction power: 31,000 pa | Disposal: Self-emptying base station for dirt and liquid | Run time: 210 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors, camera | Filtration: Yes | Mopping: Yes, hot water cleaning | Child lock: Yes

Narwal’s Flow 2 has enough suction power to yank pet hair out of deep-pile rugs and carpets, and its mopping is so good it has kept my floors squeaky clean despite the best efforts of my five dogs (two of whom love to dig and track in dirt). Especially handy is its ability to automatically detect stains and other messes, then adjust its settings while cleaning that spot, rather than having to run the whole cleaning job at max strength. The newest addition to my fur family isn’t housebroken yet, so I’ve been relying on that feature to clean spots I may have missed while working.

But I don’t have to run a full cleaning job every time my dog has an accident, as you can set custom zones. All you have to do is drag your finger over the portion of the map you want the robot to clean, configure your settings, and let the robot run. Depending on how dirty your pets tend to leave your floors — the more outdoor adventures, walks, or trips to the park, the more outside gunk they’ll likely bring in — you can fine-tune the specifics of your vacuum’s cleaning job. The Flow 2 can be programmed to vacuum and mop your floors from one to three times, and there are options to change the vacuum’s suction power and how much water it uses when mopping. And in addition to smart object detection, this robot also has pet detection, so you don’t have to worry about it charging at your skittish animal.

Beyond being good for managing households with a lot of pet hair, the Flow 2 excels at cleaning up fine particles that can seep into a rug or carpet. For instance, I poured a handful of coffee grounds on my carpet and had the Flow do a quick cleaning job over that spot. After it had run over the spot just once, I couldn’t tell any coffee grounds had been there at all.

Brushes: Single-brush system | Suction power: 3,200 pa | Disposal: Manually emptied bag with diaper salts | Run time: 180 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors, camera | Filtration: Yes | Mopping: Yes | Child lock: Yes

If you don’t need the Flow 2’s high suction power for things like sucking fur out of deep-pile carpets, the Matic’s more privacy-friendly software, charming design, and smell-free dirt and water bag have made it one of my favorite robots to date.

You can see the Matic’s advantages from the moment you send it to start mapping your home for the first time. Unlike most other robots, which follow a straight pattern when mapping and cleaning your home, the Matic zooms around in a seemingly random pattern. It took a little under 20 minutes to map my home, while other vacuums usually take around 30. Cleaning is almost as quick. In about 45 minutes, it managed to vacuum and mop a week’s worth of dirt and hair while only getting caught once on a loose thread from a rug.

That’s all made possible by Matic’s intelligent software. It’s constantly updating its map based on what it sees as it cleans; the robot’s taller body means its 3-D maps are more detailed than maps from shorter robots. And while most other robots send their mapping data back to a company’s servers — even if that data is anonymized — everything happens locally on the Matic. Despite not feeding into a company’s object-recognition algorithm, this robot is still able to identify messier areas, like a spill on your kitchen floor, and boost its settings for more thorough cleaning.

Especially handy for pet owners: The Matic doesn’t produce the gnarly odor that some other mopping robots do. Many come with a self-emptying dock that stores dirty water after the robot’s on-unit tank gets filled. If you’re not diligent about emptying and cleaning that dock’s tank, it develops a particularly gross smell. That’s not a problem with the Matic. It has a bag inside that stores dirt, debris, and dirty water. To make sure you never have to plug your nose when emptying it, the bag is lined with diaper salts, which kill the odor. So far, I haven’t had any issues.

I do have a few gripes with the Matic. Most importantly for pet owners, its suction is significantly weaker than that of the Saros. It’s fine for pulling hairs off hardwood and short-pile carpets and rugs, but it may struggle with deeper pile rugs. Additionally, its tall body prevents it from reaching places with low clearance, such as underneath a couch or bed. Last, I’ve noticed that it’s not great at reaching the edges of rooms, so you may have to do some spot cleaning from time to time.

entry.title: The 15 Very Best Women’s Leggings
entry.summary: For running, stretching, and replying to emails.
entry.content:
Whether or not you believe in wearing them outside the house (I wouldn’t judge you either way), leggings should be the most comfortable pair of pants you own. The best ones are stretchy and formfitting without feeling restrictive, and they’re made from high-quality materials that can withstand hundreds of wash and dry cycles without wearing out. To find options for different activities (from lounging to traveling to CrossFit), I spoke with athleisure designers and consultants about which features to look for and which brands to trust. Then I tested out their recommendations for myself. All of the leggings below are stretchy enough to exercise in, but I’ve also written a stand-alone guide to the best yoga pants if you’re spending a lot of time on the mat.

Updated on October 30, 2026
I updated prices and checked stock for all products and added new pairs of leggings from Quince, Athleta, and the Frankie Shop.

Leggings should feel like a second skin when you’ve got them on, so the best brands will offer an extensive size range to ensure that everyone gets a good fit. I’ve noted the available sizing for each of our recommended pairs below.

Leggings are typically constructed from a blend of either nylon and spandex or polyester and spandex. Slightly more durable than polyester, nylon is also more expensive. Polyester is still a great choice and highly effective at wicking sweat away from your skin while exercising.

Elastane (also referred to as spandex or Lycra) is what makes leggings stretchy and comfortable compared to regular pants. “The higher the percentage, the more stretch the fabric will have,” explains Shadi Adada, the co-founder of FittDesign. High-elastane leggings are also more compressive, supporting muscles and enhancing blood flow while you exercise. Most leggings these days claim to have “four-way stretch,” but this is essentially just a marketing term that refers to a high percentage of elastane.

In general, low-compression leggings are best for wearing around the house, medium-compression leggings are great for yoga and Pilates, and high-compression leggings are ideal for running and high-intensity exercise. If you’re exercising (or just prefer a less jiggly look) a percentage of at least 18 percent elastane is ideal, says Souad Acha, co-founder of Stateless Fashion Design and Consulting.

I’ve taken note of whether or not each pair of leggings listed here has pockets. For lounging around at home, walking the dog, or running, pockets are ideal — they “allow you to easily store your keys and phone when you need use of both hands,” says Acha. But yogis I’ve spoken with tend to prefer pocket-free pants. “Anything with extra seams, zippers, or buttons is distracting because you’re rolling around on the floor a lot,” says Sky Ting yoga co-founder Krissy Jones.

Size range: 0 to 14 | Fabric: 81 percent nylon, 19 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | Pockets: Two side pockets

Lululemon’s leggings are a significant investment but one that I — as well as fellow Strategist staffers and numerous fitness experts we’ve spoken with over the years — have found to be worth it. While the brand’s Wunder Train pants are my favorite for yoga, these Align leggings are thinner and more flexible, which makes them more comfortable to wear while lounging. They’re also ideal maternity wear: Strategist contributing editor Jessica Silvester wore them while seven months pregnant and says the same pair snapped back into shape and still fits her regular proportions years later.

Size range: XS to 3XL | Fabric: 82 percent nylon, 18 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | Pockets: Waistband pocket, two side pockets

So what’s the difference between $33 and $98 leggings, anyway? The Lululemon Align fabric above looks and feels smoother than Baleaf’s and has stronger lines of reinforced stitching at the seams. But after extensive testing, I’ve found that both brands hold up well in the dryer and will last for years without shrinking or warping in shape. Baleaf’s leggings are affordable yet comfortable, even if they don’t look as nice as expensive brands. As Strategist contributor Maggie Slepian puts it, they’re “right between the compression levels of more supportive tights (which can feel too restrictive for all-day wear) and supersoft leggings (which can sag and lose their shape).” So you can work out in them or work from home in them. Which is not so much the case with ultracompressive leggings that have a higher elastane percentage.

Size range: XXS to 4XL | Fabric: 95 percent cotton, 5 percent elastane (ribbed legging), 90 percent cotton, 10 percent elastane (foldover pant) | Compression: Very low | Pockets: None

I prefer to wear nonathletic leggings around the house — no shiny compression pants while I’m watching Hacks, thanks. If you feel the same, Skims leggings are slinky and comfortable. Fitness guru Tracy Anderson told us she’s obsessed with her cotton ribbed ones: “I wear them with a cashmere sweater — that’s my uniform.” Strategist senior editor Hilary Reid and deputy editor Simone Kitchens prefer the brand’s breezier foldover leggings, which Reid says are “ideal for putting on if I’m rolling out of bed and doing some kind of at-home mat workout in the morning before work.” She adds that while the foldover waistband evokes the early-aughts trends she coveted as a teen, “as a now-30-something, I will say it’s actually kind of utilitarian in that you can adjust the ‘rise’ of the pants depending on how you feel that day.”

Size range: XS to XL | Fabric: 85 percent polyester, 15 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | Pockets: Optional

Resident Strategist writer and runner Brenley Goertzen tried on all the leggings from Quince, and these were her favorites because they feel like cotton even though they’re made from a polyester fabric that the brand refers to as Ultra-Soft. “These are my pick if you’re looking for a pair of leggings you can comfortably wear all day, since they are plenty stretchy but also have a brushed, cottonlike softness,” she says. “The extra-thick waistband stays in place nicely, doesn’t dig into my hips, and keeps everything sucked in.”

Size range: XXS to L | Fabric: 87 percent polyester, 13 percent elastane | Compression: Low | Pockets: None

A put-together pair of leggings is hard to find. My fellow Strategist writer Lauren Ro is very particular about wearing athleisure outside the house, and as much as she adores her Lulu Aligns, “they’re slightly too unstructured to comfortably wear around town.” She searched for a pair of leggings with a soft feel that were smoothing and supportive (but not too sporty-looking) and settled on these. “They have a bit more compression than the Aligns without being too tight, giving me more definition and, let’s be honest, confidence,” she says. “I wore them with Spanx’s AirEssentials Half Zip to dim sum with the family and felt like a polished Pilates mom — even though I was unshowered and had bits of har gow in my hair.”

Size range: XXS to 3XL | Fabric: 75 percent polyester, 25 percent elastane | Compression: High | Pockets: One back pocket

Speaking of sweat, these Athleta leggings are made from moisture-wicking polyester along with Lycra, making them optimal for high-intensity exercise. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio picked up her first pair of Elation tights during a Black Friday sale in 2022 and has been wearing them (mainly to work out and coach a girls’ soccer team) ever since. Compared to the Lululemon Aligns, “they are a little more compressive,” she says, as well as thicker. This creates a smoothing effect, and she feels more comfortable wearing them in public. The waistband “never rolls,” and the back waistband pocket will handily fit a smartphone if needed. She owns eight pairs of these in different variations; the Ultra High Rise is her favorite.

Size range: XS to XL | Fabric: 92 percent cotton, 8 percent elastane | Compression: High | Pockets: Available with or without

This year I went on a quest to find natural-fiber workout gear, which is happily becoming a more mainstream concept as we cut back on global plastic consumption. I was first drawn to Mate’s tights because they both look and feel familiar. Some cotton workout leggings can be a little baggy, but these closely resemble a pair of sleek and compressive polyester yoga pants. The weave is tight and thick enough to mimic a synthetic fabric, the wide waistband compresses your abs, reinforced seams on the sides provide structure, and there’s plenty of stretch. The remarkably smooth cotton sculpts your body somewhat but remains breathable — unlike polyester, which often makes me overheat. I was particularly struck by how well-made these leggings are. There are no loose threads, and the stitching is even. Much more so than other options, they seem explicitly designed for high-intensity workouts. I was able to go running in mine without having to stop and pull them up or adjust the fit and found them just as comfortable as my nylon leggings for Pilates. They did bunch a bit around the ankles; if you’re short like me, definitely opt for the midi rather than full length.

Size range: XS to XL | Fabric: 77 percent polyester, 23 percent elastane | Compression: High | Pockets: Front and back waistband pockets, side pockets

Goertzen loves these leggings that have streamlined her training sessions by letting her leave the house without a running belt. They have a built-in belt around the waistband with enough space for her phone, keys, gels, AirPods, and even a few treats if she’s jogging with her dog. And there are still two drop-in side pockets on both legs for even more storage. Convenience aside, these are also just a great pair of exercise leggings, with high compression and a tight fabric weave that wicks sweat away from the body.

Size range: XXS to 6XL | Fabric: 79 percent RPET, 11 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | Pockets: One back pocket

I’m not exactly sure how Girlfriend Collective manages to turn plastic bottles into pants, but the result is unusually comfortable and stylish. These yoga pants are a hit among Strategist staffers as well as athletes and yogis we’ve spoken to over the years, including Jones, who calls them “by far the most sustainable” leggings that are “still concerned with fit and look.” Health-care entrepreneur Hil Moss, a breast-cancer survivor who has undergone a mastectomy and rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, says that they made the process just a bit easier: “I have multiple pairs in different colors. That’s how much I love them.”

Size range: XXS to XXL | Fabric: 96 percent acrylic, polyester, and rayon; 4 percent elastane | Compression: Very low | Pockets: None

I like to wear Uniqlo’s Heattech leggings around the house during winter, when central heating is doing most of the work but I still want an extra boost of warmth. They’ve also come in handy while waiting for the Q train in cold and windy subway tunnels. Over the years, numerous fashion insiders have told us that they love their Heattech layers too; celebrity stylist Krisana Sotelo is a fan, and so is Richer Poorer co-founder Iva Pawling, who ran to purchase a pair during an unexpected freezing-cold NYC trip. “They were easy to wear under jeans and saved my built-for-70-degrees self,” she says.

Size range: 2XS to 2XL | Fabric: 74 percent polyamide, 26 percent elastane | Compression: High | ﻿Pockets: None

Strategist contributor Katie Stone, who has tried all the activewear brands, recently did a 180 on Vuori’s popular leggings. She especially recommends this drawstring pair, which she says will stay perfectly positioned during whatever sort of reformer-Pilates gymnastics position you find yourself in. The fabric is thick and structured, so they’re ideal for colder weather and higher impact activities, but the drawstring also means that you can loosen things up a bit when lounging at home.

Size range: XS to XL | Fabric: 90 percent Supplex, 10 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | ﻿Pockets: None

While most leggings are utilitarian-looking at best, Live the Process’s ballet-inspired designs manage to be “shockingly beautiful,” as Jones puts it. “If anyone wants to splurge on the nicest yoga pants out there, their shapes and colors are amazing,” she says. “So is the quality of the material.” Strategist senior writer Liza Corsillo, who has been wearing the same pair of Live the Process leggings for close to a decade, agrees. The brand’s stirrup leggings were first recommended to me by dancer Angela Trimbur, who came across them while receiving breast-cancer treatments a few years ago. “I spent a lot of time at home resting in blah-looking basics that left me feeling extra blah,” she recalls. “I realized that investing in chicer looks to rest in made me feel more confident, hopeful, and happy.” These days, she wears them while dancing in her home studio and then tosses street clothes over the top to run errands.

Size range: XXS to XL | Fabric: 100 percent merino wool | Compression: Low | ﻿Pockets: None

When Strategist contributing writer Laura Neilson went on a skeptical hunt for the best stirrup leggings, she fell in love with this ribbed pair from the Frankie Shop. She’s always “genuinely excited” to wear them because they’re made entirely from merino wool, which gives them “the same pull-on ease as a beloved ribbed turtleneck.” This means that they’re most ideal for lounging around in when it’s sweater weather and shouldn’t be worn for exercise. “I’d wear them for weekend errands as a stylish alternative to sweatpants, maybe with an oversize chunky sweater,” Neilson adds.

Size range: XXS to L | Fabric: 87 percent nylon, 13 percent elastane | Compression: Low | Pockets: None

Flared yoga pants are both trendy and versatile; what I especially like about Alo’s Airbrush ones is that they’re constructed from a soft and stretchy matte fabric rather than the more traditional shiny yoga-pant material. This means they really do work as (very comfortable and flattering) everyday pants if you throw a T-shirt over the top. I tried both the flared and bootcut styles and would advise the latter if you favor a subtle ’90s look over a more billowy ’70s one.

entry.title: Jones Road’s Color Corrector Is the Difference Between Good and Great Makeup
entry.summary: It’s one more step, but it makes a huge difference in your makeup.
entry.content:
For years, color correcting was one of those makeup techniques that I knew I should do but never did. It always seemed a bit advanced for my otherwise simple makeup routine and just one more step in the process. Then Jones Road launched a color corrector this fall — Wide Awake Brightening Neutralizer — along with its new Wide Awake Brightening Concealer, a separate product that is meant to be applied before the concealer to correct discoloration. Fine, I’ll try it, I thought, because I typically like Jones Road products. When I looked back at pictures from the event I wore it to, I could see that my skin tone looked more cohesive and my makeup looked more finished than it usually does. Since then, I’ve been color correcting my under eyes regularly and also dabbing the product on broken capillaries around my face before using concealer and foundation.

I suspect I’m not alone here. Most makeup wearers are probably not color correcting before concealer or foundation because it just seems too pro-level or maybe even intimidating, but it’s work worth doing, says makeup artist Daniel Martin. I asked him to break down and demystify the technique.

Most people don’t have just one tone on their face. We may have darkness under the eyes, redness around the nose or on the cheeks, or darker patches on parts of the face, and foundation isn’t necessarily going to cover it all. You may be thinking, But isn’t that what concealer is for? Yes, and concealers may cover discoloration, but sometimes those underlying blue, purple, or red areas still show through. A color corrector counteracts that tone before you add coverage. Martin admits it’s precision work, but it’s an additional step that ultimately makes the rest of your makeup look better. “If you’re someone who has dark under eyes, that’s where you want to spend your most time,” he says. “Once that’s perfected and blended, everything else is pretty easy.”

This is the intimidating part for many people, but it’s basic color theory. Color correctors come in a range of shades, including pinks, peaches, apricots, yellows, and greens. Most people benefit from a peachy tone (ranging from light to dark peaches) under the eyes, which neutralizes purply blue tones. Deep apricots are also helpful for gray tones or brown spots. It’s often said that green is best for counteracting redness, but Martin isn’t a fan. “They’re sometimes too green,” he says. Instead, he uses yellow on redness. “The yellow and red of your skin creates an orange or a peach tone, and I like bringing more warmth to the skin.”

For me, the texture of the corrector makes a difference. I’ve tried some liquid correctors that seemed too wet and slippery and just mixed in with the concealer. Hours later, I could see the peach tone under my eyes. The Jones Road neutralizer is creamy but not wet and easy to pat onto the skin without slipping around too much. Martin says the texture is really a matter of preference, and skin prep plays a bigger role in how it applies and layers.

As mentioned, skin prep matters a lot here. When I told Martin about my “too wet” corrector, he suspected that I didn’t allow the emollients in my eye cream to sink in first. So allow at least five minutes after applying serums and moisturizers before going in with a corrector. Martin likes to use his fingers, not a brush, to correct. “I like to use the heat from my hands to lay the product and keep it from looking dry or cakey,” he says. “You want it to meld; you don’t want it to just sit on your skin.” He then adds concealer and foundation. For stubborn discoloration, Martin will then go back in with the corrector over the foundation, too, and finish with a light dusting of powder to set.

This is the one I’ve been applying. It comes in nine different shades. I’m using Light Peachy Pink, which is the perfect, not-too-pink-not-too-peach shade that’s just right for my light skin.

“I recently used this on actor Naomi Akie,” says Martin. “It’s made for the eyes, but I wound up using it to correct all over her face. The dry-down was quick.”

“Huda Beauty has a nice corrector that I just started using,” says Martin. “It’s pretty wet, but the pigment dries down really fast. You can get a trial size at Sephora, which is nice if you don’t want to commit to a big one yet.”

entry.title: The 15 Very Best Slippers for Women
entry.summary: From cozy cold-weather pairs to waterproof and lightweight options.
entry.content:
Now that it has become socially acceptable to wear slippers outdoors — to the grocery store, to school, out to dinner — the market is flooded with all manner of furry, fuzzy, and cozy options. And it just so happens that furry, fuzzy, and cozy are my domain here at the Strategist. I cover our wardrobe-basics beat, which means I’ve handled dozens of the fleeciest cashmere sweaters and worn the softest worn-in white tees. To find the best slippers, I tried several different slides, moccasins, and booties. (And I’ll be testing even more this spring.) I wore them around the house on lazy, lie-around Saturdays and slid them on to check the mail and run errands. To round out the list, my colleague Arielle Avila and I spoke to a podiatrist to understand what makes a slipper actually good for your feet and interviewed people whose taste we trust to get their own takes on the best ones out there. Plus, I dug through our archives of comfy-shoe content to find our consistently recommended pairs. All of that added up to our list of the best women’s slippers for nearly any occasion — from cozy open-toe options for hot summer days to insulated fleece-lined slippers for when it’s freezing.

Updated on October 15, 2025
All of our picks for the best women’s slippers are still available, and prices have be updated to reflect the latest discounts. I’ve also added OrthoFeet’s Charlotte as our best slippers with customizable arch support.

Since slippers typically don’t come in standard sh oe sizing, we tried our best to include pairs with a wide range of sizes. We’ve noted all sizing details, below, from whether they come unisex, include half sizes, or come in wide or narrow options.

Podiatrist Dr. Asim Sayed tells us that support and protection are two of the most important qualities to look for when shopping for slippers. He prefers anything with a rubber outsole because it offers more protection, stability, and control than softer materials, which are “pretty much like big socks.” This is especially important if you’re planning to wear slippers outside (even just to grab the mail). And if you have neuropathy or are shopping for someone who has it, a firm, hard sole (like rubber) is a must. “People with neuropathy don’t feel a lot of things that someone who doesn’t have neuropathy feels,” Sayed says. “They could have a Lego in their slipper all day long and they wouldn’t even know, which leads to wounds, and that can lead to amputations or worse.”

This mostly comes down to personal preference. When stylist Savannah White shops for slippers, she looks for “breathable materials that will still insulate and keep you warm.” Meanwhile, Sayed says anyone who has a bunion will want slippers made with a forgiving lining material (like a breathable mesh) rather than an irritating fabric (like leather). Other experts we spoke to prioritized the durability and weight of their slippers, choosing uppers in sheepskin, suede, or leather.

Slippers are a broad category and come in variations from open-toe sandals to ankle-high booties. Sayed tells us a lot of this comes down to personal preference, but he notes that if you have any Achilles-tendon pain or a Haglund’s deformity (an enlargement of the bony section of the heel), it’s best to stick with an open-back shoe.

The price of slippers runs the gamut from $20 to a couple hundred dollars, depending on the materials they’re made of. We focused on worth-it slippers and their more affordable options. Every pair is denoted as either $ (under $100), $$ (under $150), or $$$ (over $150).

Sizing: 5 to 13 | Outsole material: Rubber | Upper and lining material: Wool | Design: Closed toe with open back | Price: $$

These wool slippers by the Denmark-based company Glerups, which have been praised by many Strategist writers over the years, are a perennial favorite here. Now I know why. After testing Glerups for several weeks, I found they satisfy everything I’ve been looking for in a slipper: They’re cozy and warm but never, ever sweaty. That’s exactly why they’ve unseated the UGG Coquettes as our best slippers overall. (Yes, I still love the Coquettes, but they’re simply too hot for year-round wear.)

When I first got the Glerups, a brand representative advised me to wear them for a couple of days without socks to let them mold to my feet — so I did just that. They weren’t by any means uncomfortable out of the box, but after a week they felt perfectly broken in, as if they were hugging my feet. I’m based in Minnesota, and on the chilliest days, my feet still felt bundled up but not suffocated, with or without socks on. And even though I’d been an UGGs loyalist for years, I found myself slipping the Glerups on instead, largely because of the wool lining, which is warm but sweat wicking.

While I haven’t yet worn these through the entire summer, I can tell they’re breathable enough for extra-warm days. I also find them less cumbersome than my UGGs because they’re not lined with fluffy shearling and the rubber sole is thin but still substantial. While I mainly wear these indoors, I have worn them to run quick errands around my neighborhood without any issues. (If you’re hesitant about wearing them outside, take note from publishing executive Lisa Lucas, who told us she frequently wears her high-top version of the slippers on bodega trips.)

Sizing: 5 to 15.5 | Outsole material: 20% recycled EVA, 80% EVA | Upper and lining material: 51% cotton, 42% recycled polyester, 7% polyamide upper and 100% recycled polyester lining | Design: Closed toe with open back | Price: $

Brunch, a New York–based start-up run by two brothers, launched in 2020 and sells hotel-inspired shoes. Strategist writers Kitty Guo and Erin Schwartz tested the Essential to see how they measure up against other new house slippers. Both Schwartz and Guo like that they’re durable, warm but not stuffy, and supportive but not orthopedic. “I’d usually switch from house slippers to my Crocs for quick trips down to my apartment building’s lobby, but these seem sturdy enough for outside wear,” says Schwartz. Guo, who has wide feet, especially likes that they’re “really roomy,” she says. “I was even able to wear thick socks with them.”

Sizing: 5 to 12 | Outsole material: Cork-infused rubber | Upper and lining material: Sheepskin with shearling lining | Design: Closed toe with open back | Price: $$

The Glerups may have unseated these UGGs as our top choice, but let’s face it: A pair of UGGs is the quintessential cozy shoe, and with the brand’s shearling-lined offerings ranging from scuff slippers to boots, there’s something for everyone. The Coquettes stand out because they’re easy to slide on but don’t flop around (thanks to the extra-fluffy lining). If you prefer an indoor-outdoor slipper, these are an excellent option. Because these have a structured, thick rubber sole, Avila says she has accidentally worn them out while grabbing mail or running to the bodega without noticing (until she gets home and realizes she needs to wipe them down). I’ve spotted them on customers at my neighborhood coffee spot, and they didn’t look as though they’d just rolled out of bed. Avila’s pair still looks brand new after plenty of wear through the colder months. They come in a wide range of sizes and colors (including neutrals and pastels) and make an excellent gift for teens who covet the brand or for anyone else who appreciates a supportive, comfortable slipper.

Sizing 4 to 12.5 | Outsole material: Latex | Outer and lining material: Wool with shearling lining | Design: Closed toe with open back | Price: $

These Birkenstocks are made with an outer wool layer and lined with shearling, and they are about $20 less than the UGGs I mentioned above. Because they’re recommended by my colleague Emma Wartzman (who liked them so much she gifted a pair to her mom), I decided to test them for myself. They’re much less fluffy than the UGGs, with a more streamlined look similar to the Glerups, but they’re still super-warm. They also have decent arch support that aligns with the rest of Birkenstock’s offerings, though I find these more lightweight. Wartzman notes that her feet feel good even after standing in the kitchen cooking for hours. Like the UGGs, these can double as an outdoor slipper; I’ve accidentally worn them out on a walk around my neighborhood with my dog, and my feet actually felt pretty stable in the footbed, even when we were moving at a faster pace. Actress Tawny Cypress has told us she frequently wears hers out to lunch. They’re so comfortable that I often forget I have them on and go the entire day working from home without taking them off.

Sizing: 5 to 10 | Outsole material: Rubber | Upper and lining material: 17mm sheepskin with shearling lining | Design: Closed toe with open back | Price: $$$

Last year, Cozy Earth launched its Puffy Sheep Slippers, and after seeing how luxurious they looked online — almost an entire shoe wrapped in plush shearling — I decided to request a sample. During the winter in Toronto, they’ve become my go-to pair of house shoes. Right out of the box, I was happy to find that they came in a cloth dust bag for storage, and after only a few wears, the fuzzy lining molded to my feet. I’m always excited to slip these on during dreary early mornings, and they make taking my puppy out at 4 a.m. for bathroom breaks much more bearable. The sheepskin is naturally odor-resistant and breathable, and while I typically wear mine with socks, I haven’t had any sweaty feet issues. I love that these have the fluffy closed-toe upper and a grippy monochromatic rubber outsole. Though I’ve only worn mine while working from home or visiting the mailroom in the lobby of my condo building, I think these should work fine for a quick errand or grabbing coffee down the street. If you’re between sizes, I recommend sizing up so there’s enough room for chunky socks.

Sizing: 5 to 11 with regular and wide options | Outsole material: Thermoplastic rubber | Outer and lining material: Sheepskin, shearling lining | Design: Closed toe | Price: $

If moccasins are more your style, L.L.Bean makes a classic, durable option. I haven’t tested these out myself, but social-content manager Siraad Dirshe says her pair has held up after years of indoor and outdoor wear. Like the other shearling-lined options, these are warm yet sweat-wicking. These are made with a shearling-covered EVA-memory-foam insole for extra comfort. They come in ten different colorways and in either regular or wide sizing options.

Sizing: 5 to 11 | Outsole material: Rubber | Upper and lining material: Suede and sheepskin lining | Design: Closed toe with adjustable high ankle | Price: $

For an even warmer option, Strategist senior writer Liza Corsillo’s cold-weather slippers of choice are these cozy booties from Minnetonka. The ankle-high sheepskin collar can be rolled up or down, so they can double as a slipper, too. Corsillo exclusively wears her pair during the winter months, and after three years, they still look new. While she uses hers indoors, these are designed for both indoor and outdoor use with a durable rubber sole. They come in black, tan, and gray colors in both regular and wide sizes.

Sizing: 5 to 11 | Outsole material: Rubber | Outer and lining material: Recycled P.E.T. outer with fleece lining | Design: Closed toe with elastic collapsible heel | Price: $

For another winter-appropriate slipper, consider these insulated North Face ones — which have a fleece lining — that I’ve worn through the coldest months of the year in both Minnesota and Toronto. They’re incredibly comfortable; the sole is quite cushy, and the soft fleece makes it feel like you’re slipping your feet into little pillows. The outer ripstop polyester features a durable water-repellent coating, making these ideal for drizzly conditions, as well. They aren’t the greatest for heavy downpours or large puddles, but they performed nicely in light rain and snow, and had enough traction even on icy sidewalks. I usually wear mine with socks, and they’ve become a favorite for wearing around the house, taking my dog outside for a quick bathroom break, or running a nearby errand. The heel is also technically collapsible, which means you can wear them more like traditional slippers, too.

Avila is also a North Face fan. “My sister gifted them to me for Christmas during our first New York winter, after months of watching me fumble around in half-slipped-on tennis shoes to grab the mail or run to the bodega,” she says. While they’re not her house slippers, they make quick trips to the store a much more pleasant experience, especially on frigid days. Stylist Lilli Millhiser also owns a pair and wears them mainly indoors; she appreciates that they’re cozy and don’t attract her dog’s hair thanks to the outer P.E.T. material.

Sizing: 5 to 11 | Outsole material: Rubber | Upper and lining material: Wool | Design: Closed toe with open back | Price: $

Giesswein, an Austrian heritage brand that’s been around for over 50 years, is known for offering generous arch support. I haven’t tested a pair, but former Strategist writer Karen Iorio-Adelson confirmed that the best-selling Veitsch slippers are ideal for anyone who likes an exaggerated arch. The rest of the slipper is made of soft virgin wool and a thick rubber sole that’s durable enough for venturing outdoors. It comes in four colorways: black, red, gray, and blue.

Sizing: 5 to 14 | Outsole material: Rubber | Upper and lining material: Wool | Design: Closed-toe with open back | Price: $$

Similar to Birkenstocks with a cork footbed, Fulton’s slippers have an extremely moldable sole with deep heel cups. I’ve been testing them for the past four months and love how lightweight they are while still supporting my feet (I’ve struggled with bouts of painful plantar fasciitis in the past). They prevent my overpronating arches from becoming aggravated when I’m walking on our hardwood floors at home. Fulton also sells insoles, and like the insoles, these slippers take a few wears to break in. The brand suggests around ten hours of consistent wear to fully break them in, so I worked up to this, adding an hour or so each day, and they eventually formed to my arches. The wool material of the upper part of the slipper is temperature regulating, and compared to other wool slippers I’ve tried, the Fulton upper is thinner and more breathable. If you prefer to wear thick socks, I recommend sizing up as these do run slightly small.

Sizing: 5 to 12 | Outsole material: Rubber | Upper and lining material: faux fur interior | Design: Closed-toe with open back | Price: $

If you’re dealing with foot pain, arthritis, or mobility challenges, and want a slipper that comes as close to a custom medical orthotic as possible, Orthofeet is your best bet. These suede Charlotte slippers have an adjustable side strap that opens wide and a heel lip to keep them securely on your foot. I mainly wear socks with all my slippers, but when I’ve accidentally gone barefoot in these the faux-fur lining (that even covers the insole) is super-soft and comfortable. These have the same podiatrist-designed Ortho-Cushion System and roomy toe box as other Orthofeet shoes, so you can easily customize the built-in orthotic insole with the included spacers and arch booster. I’ve suffered from plantar fasciitis for years, and when I’m not wearing house shoes, I almost always experience a flare-up from walking or standing on our hard wood floors. The Charlotte slippers have solid arch support and the heel cup is incredibly stable. When I first slipped them on, I noticed an instant pressure relief, and they require zero break-in period. I love them so much that I might have to buy a second pair: one for wearing around the block while walking my dogs and the other for only around the house.

Sizing: 5 to 16 | Outsole material: Proprietary OOfoam | Upper and lining material: Proprietary OOfoam | Design: Open toe with one strap | Price: $

While these Oofos slides are far from traditional house slippers, they’re so comfortable and supportive they deserve a spot on this list. Avila wears hers casually in the warmer months, usually on trips to the beach, and says, “I feel as if I could walk for days in them.” This is probably chalked up to its design and its proprietary “OOfoam“: The slippers are made to reduce stress on joints and absorb more impact. SuChin Pak, who wears hers at home exclusively, adds that the extra-thick sole makes walking a little wobbly at first and forces you to put pressure on different points of your foot, which in turn reduces stress on sore feet, knees, and lower backs. Two other folks who’ve recommended the slippers in the past — photographer Erin Patrice O’Brien and Strategist columnist Chris Black — say these are great for people with plantar fasciitis and high arches. “They mold to the foot, and the arch support is excellent,” says Black. “Your gait will thank you!”

Sizing: 5 to 11 | Outsole material: EVA | Upper and lining material: Recycled bamboo | Design: Closed toe with open back | Price: $$

If you prefer a closed-toe slipper that won’t lead to sweaty feet, turn to Lusso Cloud’s Pelli slippers. Guo, who owns a pair herself, says they’re more breathable than the aforementioned Brunch pair because of their construction and material. The upper is made from waffle-knit recycled bamboo stretched over perforated memory foam, promoting air circulation. And, the “Triple Stack Technology” footbed, which consists of three layers of foam. The Pelli comes in the widest range of options, including pairs made with suede, terrycloth, leather, and polyester upper materials, and others with shearling lining if you do want a cold-weather pair.

Sizing: S to L | Outsole: Plastic | Upper and lining: Cotton waffle weave | Design: Closed toe with open back | Price: $

Hawkins New York — makers of our favorite quilts, cloth napkins, and linen sheets — also makes an excellent under-$50 pair of slippers. When Avila tested them in a size small, she appreciated how roomy and breathable they felt. Throughout the summer, her feet never got too sweaty when she wore them with or without socks. They have nice traction thanks to their grippy outsoles too. Another plus is that they come in 12 colors, including neutrals and earth tones.

Sizing: 5 to 13 | Outsole: Rubber | Upper and lining: RWS-certified Merino wool | Design: Closed-toe with open back | Price: $$

I kept spotting these knit clogs on fashion influencers, and when the brand finally restocked my size, I ordered them immediately. The major appeal of all Rothy’s shoes, including this style, is that they’re machine washable, which was a huge draw for me (especially considering how many times I’ve accidentally dripped coffee on my UGGs). Though they’re named the Casual Clogs, I view them as slippers because they’re backless and have a flat sole. I wear mine without socks when I’m working from home, often at my standing desk, and am always impressed with the cushy yet supportive footbed that never makes my arches feel tired in the way other slippers have. My Casual Clogs required zero break-in period, and I found the merino wool plenty breathable for year-round wear, even when paired with thick, slouchy socks. Just note: These run large, so if you’re between sizes like I am, you should definitely size down.

entry.title: I’ve Squeezed into All Kinds of Shapewear. This Is the Best.
entry.summary: Spanx isn’t the only option, but it’s a favorite for a reason.
entry.content:
First things first: There’s nothing wrong with not wearing shapewear, which has a reputation for being uncomfortable — the phrase “sausage casing” came up often in interviews for this guide. But I like to think of it as a secret weapon (and a bit of a confidence booster) for smoothing out my curves, giving me some lift, and hiding possible panty lines, so I feel my best in whatever I’m wearing.

Plus, the industry has gone through big changes in the last five or so years: Much of today’s shapewear is meant to be comfortable enough to wear every day, and lots of brands have made their lines more inclusive, with fits for different body types and a range of skin-tone shades. There’s also a lot more competition in the market: Kim Kardashian–founded Skims is a formidable Spanx rival, and start-ups like Shapermint abound.

So to find the best shapewear, I put together a panel of experts — including underwear-store owners, plus-size bloggers, and Hollywood costume designers — and asked them about their favorites. Then I started trying their recommendations myself, wearing them under anything figure-hugging to judge their level of comfort and see how smoothing and supportive they really are. Or if you’re shopping for more underthings, we have guides to the best underwear and lingerie as well.

Updated on October 30, 2026
Our new favorite shapewear is the Skims Cool Shapewear Mid Thigh Bodysuit, while our former best overall, the Skims Seamless Sculpt Brief Bodysuit, now takes second place. We updated prices and checked stock for every other shapewear piece here.

Getting the right size makes all the difference in shapewear — a piece that’s too big won’t do much smoothing, and one that’s too small will be squeezing. Whenever possible, I highlighted the brands offering a wide range of sizes. Some of the shapewear below starts at XS and goes as high as 8X, with a few pieces using band-and-cup bra sizing instead of lettered sizing.

I included a mix of slips, shorts, thongs, tanks, and bodysuits, and made sure to mention features like whether a piece of shapewear comes with a built-in bra or is cut as a thong or a brief. The type you choose will determine its effect — whether that’s shaping your thighs, stomach, butt, or whole body.

Some shapewear is going to be a little bit uncomfortable, especially if it’s a full-coverage piece that compresses your entire torso — “you’ll likely not want to endure them for more than an evening,” says stylist Jessica Cadmus. But even if you’re willing to put up with some squeeze, “it should never be so tight that you feel like you’re suffocating underneath your clothes,” explains Shammara Lawrence, founder of the Power of Plus. However, there’s a lot of shapewear on the market now that feels stretchier and forgiving enough to wear day-to-day. To judge comfort, I ranked each recommendation below on a scale of 1 to 3 — with 1 being as comfortable as shapewear can get with more minimal shaping; 2 feeling tighter but bearable; and 3 being the tightest and least comfortable but most effective with the highest level of shaping. These numbers are based on my own testing and what those I talked to said.

Sizes: XXS–4X | Type: Bodysuit with a scoop neckline and mid-thigh shorts | Comfort and shaping level: 1

Kim Kardashian knows how to make, as our friends at The Cut have said, “maddeningly good shapewear.” Skims, founded in 2019, is one of the most size-inclusive lines in the shapewear space today — even compared to well-established brands like Spanx, Commando, and Wacoal. And nearly every piece of shapewear it makes — including bodysuits, bras, shorts, and underwear — is available in a range of “nudes” with names like sand, cocoa, and espresso. That’s all to say that it’s hard to beat Skims when it comes to shapewear; our former best overall, the brand’s Seamless Sculpt Brief Bodysuit, was only just defeated by its Cool Shapewear Mid Thigh Bodysuit.

The Cool Shapewear Mid Thigh Bodysuit is as comfortable as shapewear gets. Maybe that has something to do with it being in Skims’s Cool Shapewear line, which is made with a moisture-wicking fabric (a polyamide-elastane blend). It also helps that it’s ranked “light” in Skims’s compression-level scale, which goes up to “extra-strong.” Wearing it doesn’t involve squeezing or pressing on your insides, but it still smooths everything out. You don’t have to worry about unseemly lines, either. If you’d like more lift, I’d wear it with a bra, but you can get away without one. To me, the whole point of shapewear is to feel your best, and that’s exactly what this does. Better yet, it has saved me from thigh chafing, affectionately known as “chub rub” — that’s priceless.

Sizes: XXS–4X | Type: Bodysuit with brief | Comfort and shaping level: 2

The Seamless Sculpt Brief Bodysuit, formerly our best overall, is now our less-expensive best overall. I think the Seamless Sculpt Brief Bodysuit provides more shaping than the Cool Shapewear Mid Thigh Bodysuit — and that’s why it’s a 2 on the comfort scale. It’s described as “strong” in Skims’s compression scale, and the brand suggests your usual size for maximum tightening or sizing up for comfort’s sake. I’d personally suggest sizing up, as I’ve found the bodysuit runs small. With that said, don’t be too scared by how tiny it looks coming out of the box, because this thing really stretches. It’s less comfortable than Cool Shapewear Mid Thigh Bodysuit, but that’s not to say that it’s uncomfortable — just beware that there will be some wiggling involved to get it on. As promised, it’s contouring and lifting — my butt isn’t flattened. I don’t wear underwear with it, and again, sizing up helps keep everything in place. And I appreciate that it’s nothing like the girdles my grandma wore. “It looks as though you’re wearing a skin-colored leotard, not some torturous contraption,” said our former writer Chloe Anello, who first tested it out for a previous version of this story.

Sizes: 34B–40DD | Type: Bodysuit with a built-in underwire bra and brief | Comfort and shaping level: 1

If you want the lacy look of the +Body Powersuit but don’t want to spend three figures, this Bali number rings up at just $60 (or even less on Amazon, depending on your size) and comes recommended by celebrity stylist Ali Levine, who says it fulfills the “the four F’s: fit, form, fabric, and fashion.” She describes the bodysuit’s peekaboo lace as “very sexy as well as slimming and trimming for the body.” There’s also a bit of breathability with the lace, and the built-in underwire bra provides good support.

Sizes: 34C–40DDD | Type: Bodysuit with built-in minimizer bra and brief | Comfort and shaping level: 1

Wacoal’s Visual Effects Bodysuit is one of the best bodysuits I’ve tried, hands down. If it came in a bigger size range — it’s only made for bra sizes 34C to a 40DDD — it might’ve even earned the “best overall” title. But I still think it deserves a spot on this list for people with larger breasts. The bodysuit features my minimizer bra of choice, the Wacoal Visual Effects, for a piece of shapewear that is lifting and lessening without making me feel like my breasts are uncomfortably smooshed. I don’t feel like I’m in some corset-tightening scene from Pride and Prejudice while putting it on. I know some shaping is happening, but I don’t really feel it — the bodysuit works with my whole figure rather than against it. It’s easy to shimmy out of the bodysuit too, with no red marks to report.

Sizes: 32D–40C | Type: Bodysuit with underwire cups, back strays, and brief | Comfort and shaping level: 3

Levine recommends this strapless bodysuit from TC Fine Intimates as a “perfect foundation” that will smooth your stomach, waist, and back while suiting different necklines, as it’s cut in a sweetheart shape at the top. “I’ve used it for awards shows like the Emmys and Oscars,” she says. You select your size based on your bra size instead of what would best fit your torso, with the bodysuit available in sizes 32B to 40C. Because it’s labeled “extra firm” — with underwire cups and “stays” (see here) for back support — you’re probably going to feel that it’s tight at first. But Levine thinks the bodysuit is bearable for a formal event where you’d like to pull out all the stops. It also comes with a set of bra straps that you can attach for versatility, if you’re wearing it under a dress or top with more coverage and want additional support.

Sizes: XS–XL | Type: Bodysuit with a plunge, low back, and mid-thigh shorts | Comfort and shaping level: 2

As Levine says, “We all think of Spanx when we hear ‘shapewear.’” The company first earned a following for its bodysuits, which were some of the only comfortable shapewear for the longest time. This version lets you show some skin, with deep plunges in both the front and the back that make it work well with low-cut necklines and backless dresses while still smoothing your waist and the small of your back.

I’d compare the feel of this bodysuit to an all-over sports bra — it’s pretty uniformly compressive. Be prepared to do some adjusting to get the right fit: Though it features padded cups, you can’t select your cup size. I had to play around with the straps and the position of the cups to make sure all the roundness of my breasts was reined in. I wear a 36D, and eventually, I got the top to feel supportive and secure so that I didn’t fear popping out from the top. But because it’s pretty plunging, I don’t think it would be as supportive for those with even bigger breasts. (And if that’s you, the bodysuit below might work better, since it lets you wear your own bra.)

Sizes: XS–3X | Type: Bodysuit with bust opening and shorts | Comfort and shaping level: 1.5

If you would rather wear your own bra, try an open-bust bodysuit. The OnCore from Spanx hides the outline of a bra well: It’s cut to curve around cups and comes up high on the sides of the bust and in the back, so there’s no hint of band or bulge from a hook-and-eye closure. It features the same torso and thigh sculpting as the Suit Your Fancy above, though this version feels lighter and more breathable despite being made from the same blend of stretchy nylon and elastane. The fabric just doesn’t feel as thick here. Because the bodysuit is more of a full-coverage style, running from under the bust to the middle of the thighs, “you might get a little tired of wearing it after a full day,” says stylist Grace Thomas, but she says the fabric feels very smooth and promises “it won’t be something you’ll want to remove the instant you put it on.” You can also get a panty version of the bodysuit, which stylist Alison Deyette says her clients tend to like better for getting a similar shaping effect with less material.

Sizes: XS–XL | Type: Slip | Comfort and shaping level: 1

Commando’s underwear is known for its true-to-the-name, gone-commando fit, and though I have only worn this slip once so far under a dress with a full skirt, I was impressed with how invisible it feels. The material is slinky microfiber on the outside and comfortable-on-the-skin cotton on the inside, hence the “two-faced” title. Cadmus says her clients appreciate the seamlessness of the slip, which is “basically undetectable to the eye” and about as comfortable as shapewear gets. Because the slip is only lightly lined and doesn’t have cups or an underwire, I felt like I needed to wear a bra with it, but you may feel differently depending on your cup size and the look you’re going for.

Sizes: S–8X | Type: Shorts | Comfort and shaping level: 2

My pick for the best shaping shorts is this pair from Rago, because it’s available in more sizes than any of the shapewear on this list, from a size small to an 8X. Costume designer Alison Freer loves the brand’s whole line, going so far as to call its bodysuit “a testament to what proper garment construction can do for the female form.” She says these shorts are a standout because they’re high-waisted (“anything that cuts you off in the middle of your midriff won’t be able to do much real shaping”), with shaping panels and contour bands to hold you in. The shorts also feature “totally flat seams that won’t ever show under clothes, a split crotch so you don’t have to wriggle out if it to use the bathroom, and special grippy, lace leg holes that don’t ride up or bind your thighs,” Freer adds. (Alternatively, if you’re in the market for shaping shorts that are compatible with thigh-high slits, Skims makes pairs to show off the right leg or the left leg, which stylist Samantha Brown describes as “ingenious.”)

Sizes: S–3X | Type: Shorts | Comfort and shaping level: 1

The Spanx Seamless Power Sculpting Mid-Thigh Short won’t cause visible panty lines, can be worn without underwear, and has a non-digging waistband, according to Sapna Palep, CEO of lingerie retailer Journelle. (She also stands behind the brand’s higher-waisted Seamless Power Sculpting High-Waisted Mid-Thigh Short that costs $2 more.) Palep likes that when she wears the shorts, they don’t feel like a heavy extra layer — they are bearable and breathable throughout the day. They “smooth out your form without changing who you are,” she says. (Another pair of shorts I heard about comes from Spanx’s diffusion collection called Assets. Stylist Ansley Morgan considers them an essential to stop her thighs from rubbing against each other.)

Sizes: S–XXXXL | Type: Shorts | Comfort and shaping level: 1

Or you could try these lighter and thinner shorts (which were featured in our guide to preventing thigh chafing) from start-up undergarment-maker Knix. Former Strategist senior writer Karen Iorio Adelson and Kara McGrath, deputy digital director at Allure, are devotees. “They’re really lightweight, so you don’t get sweaty,” Adelson says. McGrath compares them to wearing nothing, recommending them to anyone she can — “and everyone who’s bought them tells me they’re a game changer.” And Strategist writer Dominique Pariso goes for the High Rise Shaper Shorts, which are similar to the Thigh Saver but with a super-high cut that starts right under her bra. There are “no noticeable stomach lines,” and they are comfortable enough that she forgets she has them on.

Sizes: XS–XL | Type: Brief | Comfort and shaping level: 1

Undies branded as “shaping” sometimes make unwanted lines with lots of seams and panels. But stylist Erica Ball describes this pair as “relatively seamless,” even with its brief cut. They have not-so-noticeable panels throughout that “help draw everything in,” explains Ball. Made from a soft microfiber fabric, they are so comfortable that she can wear them without complaint for an entire day: “This is an easy shapewear item that gives me drastic results with little effort.” (There’s also a thong version that she has similar praise for.)

Sizes: 26–46 (equivalent to S–8X) | Type: Brief | Comfort and shaping level: 1

These Ragos are made from a breezier mesh-and-lace combo and go up to a size 46 (equivalent to an 8X on the brand’s sizing chart). Though they’re more of a granny panty than the Commandos above, they cost half as much and will still smooth your stomach. Freer likes that these are cut higher on the thighs, making them a lot more comfortable. “The only seam on this panty is cleverly hidden between the cheeks, making it invisible under clothes,” she says.

Sizes: S–XL | Type: Thong | Comfort and shaping level: 1

A shaping thong might seem like an oxymoron, but Dina Scherer, owner of Modnitsa Styling, says this lacy, high-waisted one from Cosabella will dispel “the misconception that shapewear can’t be sexy and feel great on you while doing its job.” She promises that its front panels smooth you out even with the thong’s more minimal coverage in the back. But if you’re looking for something more heavy-duty, there are different thong-style pieces from Spanx that come highly recommended too.

Sizes: XS–3X | Type: Tank with scoop neck | Comfort and shaping level: 1

Yummie is perhaps best known for its tanks, which are what Levine usually has clients wear for red-carpet and press events. “I like how soft yet fitted they are,” she says. This one features two inner panels that can be moved to the front or the back of the tank to smooth out what you want. (You can also change the neckline from a scoopneck to a V-neck by reversing the tank.) Levine especially loves it for underneath sheath dresses and blouses. Brown is also a fan and says it works just as well under clingy sweaters. She adds that the tank could even be worn on its own “with a nice pair of trousers.” And though it may be counterintuitive to how you put on normal tops, when wearing any shaping tank, remember: Step into the garment and shimmy it up.

Sizes: S–4XL |Type: Cami with scoop neck | Comfort level: 1.5

Shapermint is a newer shapewear brand that has become well known for its camisoles. I like that I can actually go braless in this one —it’s like wearing a great bralette. It really feels like I’m sucked into it, which is why I’m ranking it as in between a 1 and a 2 on the comfort-and-shaping scale. And while I wouldn’t wear the cami underneath something overly formfitting, it’s great for a dress with draping, as it’ll lie flat against the body when you want to feel a little more secure. Though I’ve shunned shaping tops in the past because they often roll up at the waist, this one stayed put through sitting and standing. I wasn’t tugging at the neckline or pulling it down. You should double-check your measurements before you buy, as the cami runs small, and the brand recommends sizing up if you’re between sizes.

entry.title: 10 Emergency-Preparedness Items for Reasonable People
entry.summary: Get ready for a power blackout, not ‘Terminator 2’
entry.content:
Doomsday prepping, once the butt of jokes and the subject of junky television documentaries, has recently gone mainstream. Even if you don’t live in an area prone to natural disaster, you’ve probably at least thought about getting some kind of go bag together — especially as governments around the world have started literally instructing people to do so.

There are a few reasons why it feels like everybody is talking about prepping right now, says Sean Gold, the founder of survival website TruePrepper. AI is the main one. “Technological advances are going at a breakneck pace,” he says. “People are looking at cybersecurity, power-grid infrastructure, and supply chains for potential disruption from AI-led or assisted disturbances.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s new Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability (FORTRESS) initiative, which aims to make U.S. military bases operational off-grid, has also got people worried, says Gold. He adds that while fears around this are likely overblown — “FORTRESS is a long-overdue Band-Aid for vulnerabilities that have long existed” — the fact that governments here and abroad seem to be passing off the responsibility of disaster preparedness to their own citizens is worth taking note of. “FEMA has been financially gutted and is a shell of what it was, which wasn’t that efficient or timely to begin with,” he says. “In times when the very people who are charged with keeping you safe are telling you to ‘get prepared,’ the rational response is prepping.”

Spending time getting to know your neighbors is probably the best way to prepare for any troubles to come because when disaster strikes, we’re all in this together. But you can also invest in a few key emergency items that don’t take up too much storage space and can double as camping gear. Whether you’re preparing for the playground scene in Terminator 2 or a brief electrical blackout, here’s a survivalist starter pack. You can also check out our guide to emergency preparedness for new homeowners as well as a more comprehensive list of the best items to stock for different kinds of emergencies.

Experts have told us you should reserve at least a seven-day supply of your prescription medications, along with any medical devices you need, in case of emergency. A good first-aid kit is also essential. Thomas Coyne, the owner and lead instructor at Thomas Coyne Survival Schools, calls Adventure Medical Kits “the best on the market.”

Leatherman’s durable multi-tools are highly praised by preppers. This one, which comes recommended by survivalist Travis McGill, is especially suitable for emergencies — it even has a whistle and fire starter alongside several types of blade.

“In an extreme global situation, an entire country may be off-grid, but someone, somewhere, will be broadcasting,” says Mykel Hawke, a former U.S. Army Special Forces captain and author of several survival books. A hand-crank radio like this one will keep you in the loop when all else fails.

Carrying both is ideal because you’ll always have a backup, but survivalists recommend lighters over matches. And it’s also worth brushing up on your fire-starting skills — it’s surprisingly tricky for beginners.

Morgan Rogue of the prepper site Rogue Preparedness prefers headlamps to flashlights and portable lanterns so you can be 100 percent hands-free and there’s less chance you’ll put your torch down and lose it.

Should you need to treat your water, gravity-fed filters are good for groups, says Hawke.

This Jackery can charge up the devices of everybody in your household, and the solar panels really work — I’ve gone camping with this setup many times.

Face masks are always useful to have stocked at home or in your go bag, whether you’re worried about forest fires, pathogens, or both. This one from Protective Health Gear is our best N95 mask overall because of its comfortable yet secure fit.

There are four classes of fire extinguishers for four kinds of fires — ordinary combustibles, grease, electrical, and metal — but your best bet is a standard home model, which is versatile and inexpensive. Strategist writer Brenley Goertzen, who recently went on an emergency-preparation journey after purchasing her first home, keeps hers under the kitchen sink.

And you should keep copies of all your important documents (e.g., a medication list and pertinent medical information, proof of address, the deed or lease to your home, passports, birth certificates, and insurance policies) ready to go, ideally in a protective case like this one.

The Strategist is designed to surface useful, expert recommendations for things to buy across the vast e-commerce landscape. Every product is independently selected by our team of editors, whom you can read about here. We update links when possible, but note that deals can expire and all prices are subject to change.
