entry.title: The Best Gaming Laptops, According to the Experts
entry.summary: How to get desktop gaming power wherever you go
entry.content:
It’s a rough time to be a gamer, and frankly, a tough time to be shopping for a serious gaming laptop. The current “RAMageddon” pricing problems we’re experiencing mean a great GPU is going to cost you 25-plus months’ worth of your World of Warcraft subscription and so will a memory upgrade. The worst part? You’ll probably want both, along with a speedy CPU.

The simple advice I’ve gleaned from the many laptop reviewers and gamers I’ve recently spoken with: Buy the best gaming laptop you can get right now so it lasts you as long as possible. But the best gaming laptop for you might not be a $5,000-plus system that’s packed with every upgrade you can get. We talked to the experts to help you find the laptop that suits your needs, whether you’re looking for extreme performance, have more modest aspirations, or you just can’t budge a penny on your budget.

The best place to put your money is the graphics card, or GPU. “Right now, gaming laptops are incredibly expensive, but typically, a higher-end GPU will last you longer if you play a lot of new games and want to play them at the best settings for years to come,” says Andrew Freedman, a senior editor at Tom’s Hardware.

If money is no object, you’ll want to opt for a laptop with a Nvidia GeForce 5090 GPU. Full stop. There simply isn’t any real competition from AMD or any other company right now.

If you’d prefer a GPU that doesn’t break the bank, the Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti still gives you 12GB of dedicated onboard memory, enough to hit high frame rates in graphically demanding titles (especially if your laptop’s display isn’t 4K). The lowest you’ll want to go is an Nvidia RTX 5060 GPU and, even then, you’ll want to make sure that you’ll be able to hit great frame rates (60-plus) in your favorite titles at the quality settings you prefer. Benchmark-focused websites like HowManyFPS or DropReference can help you figure this out.

There’s another specification you’ll want to make sure you’re looking out for: TGP, or the maximum amount of power the laptop allows the GPU to use This spec may be called something else on a laptop’s spec sheets, so just make sure you’re scanning for any information related to the laptop’s graphics power (in watts).

“It’s not just which GPU you get, it’s how much power the laptop actually gives it,” Laurence, an independent reviewer known as LADTech on YouTube, says. “Two laptops can both have an RTX 5050, but one might run it at 100 W and the other at 70 W, and you’ll see a real difference in performance between them.”

Bennet, who reviews many, many laptops as Crimson Tech on YouTube, has some hard truths for those looking to game for as little money as possible. “As for budget options, most laptops under 1,000 to 1,200 bucks are edging the border of trashy. The most important thing to look out for on cheaper options is the GPU wattage, because if that thing’s only got a single heat pipe and fan, and power limits of 45 watts on a 5060, you’re better off just not buying a gaming laptop at all.”

Also make sure whatever laptop you’re eyeballing doesn’t have any performance-throttling issues as a result of poor thermals. Check that other owners haven’t reported any serious performance issues in more reasonable conditions. As Ashley Biancuzzo, associate editor at PCWorld, puts it, a great laptop needs “a serious cooling system, too — all that heat has to go somewhere!”

“You should treat 16GB of RAM as the baseline nowadays,” says Biancuzzo. If you regularly play titles that are fairly casual or otherwise not very graphically demanding, you’ll probably be fine sticking with that. Resist the urge to drop down to 8GB no matter what it does to your gaming laptop’s price, as you run the risk of having a fairly subpar experience across everything you’ll use the laptop to do, not just games.

Conversely, if you can stomach the cost, “32GB would be perfect,” says Bennet. But, he warns, given how expensive memory is nowadays, “I’d highly advise against paying a 600-buck markup for going from 16 to 32, since most people will be perfectly fine with 16GB.”

If you want the best visual experience — accurate colors, great contrast, and deep blacks in any room condition — you’ll want to go OLED: Ideally, something that can hit 1,000 nits at peak brightness and comes with a VESA TrueBlack HDR1000 certification (or higher). A great laptop should also allow you to set it to a more modest HDR400 or HDR500 display mode, in case the laptop display’s auto-brightness limiter is driving you nuts when you’re using its HDR1000+ mode or if any of your favorite games appear washed out.

Gaming laptops typically come in one of three resolutions: 1,200p, 1,600p, or 2,400p (4K), though you can still find some gaming laptops sporting an “HD” 1,080p display. The higher the resolution, the greater the clarity, but you’ll want a larger screen to enjoy the benefits. “4K is wasted under 18 inches, IMO,” says Jon Martindale, a freelance technology journalist and reviewer for ExtremeTech, PCWorld, Micro Center, and others.

The bigger the display, the better, but that will impact your laptop’s portability — even lugging an 18-inch laptop around the house can feel like a chore. This is harder to avoid for gaming laptops than general-purpose laptops, but a decent rule of thumb is that “anything under four pounds is fine for carrying around,” Martindale says, adding, “I wouldn’t want to haul five-plus pounds with me all day.”

Also, a higher-resolution display means your GPU will need to push more pixels. A 4K laptop demands more graphics horsepower than a 1,200p laptop, which can mean spending more on a better GPU, as well as your laptop’s cooling, to get as good a gaming experience. There’s nothing wrong with shooting for the moon — a gorgeous 4K, OLED display — but you’ll need to invest more to keep those frame rates and graphical quality settings as high as they can go.

“Honestly? If someone can afford to spend thousands of dollars on [a premium gaming laptop], I’d just lean into it,” Biancuzzo says. “At that price point, you’re looking at upper-level GPUs (RTX 5080 / 5090), 1,600p OLED displays (240Hz), 32GB RAM, etc.”

As for your laptop’s refresh rate, a great gaming laptop should be able to hit 144Hz, at minimum, but you’ll often find laptops that can do much better than that. However, a 440Hz panel doesn’t give you any extra benefit if you can only output 120 frames per second in most of your games. It’s more futureproofed, sure, but if given the option, it wouldn’t hurt to pull back to a 240Hz screen (using the same panel type) if it’ll save you a little cash.

To get a gaming laptop worth its (considerable) weight, look for a mainstream Intel or AMD x64/x86 processor. Qualcomm’s ARM-based chips support some low- to medium-complexity gaming, but still have compatibility issues with too many titles to make them viable alternatives for a dedicated gaming machine.

With Intel, you’ll typically want a gaming laptop based on Intel’s Core Ultra 9 or Ultra 7 chips, preferably one based on the company’s Arrow Lake Refresh architecture, and specifically the “H” or “HX” designations, which are Intel’s mid- and top-tier offerings. An i7 or i9 based on Intel’s older 14th-generation Raptor Lake architecture is also a good choice and can save you a little money.

On the AMD side, you’ll want to target laptops using its Ryzen 9 9000-series chips for top performance (again, look for “HX”-designated chips using the company’s latest Zen 5 architecture). If you want maximum performance, aim for the 300-series Ryzen AI Max+ chip, and if you want to spend less, AMD’s 200-series Ryzen 7 chips are competitive with Intel’s “Raptor Lake” lineup.

But don’t worry too hard about your CPU. When in doubt, spend more money on a better GPU, if you have to pick. “The CPU upgrades are nice, but not as meaningful,” says Freedman. He adds: “If you’re willing to go a generation or two back on the CPU, you may find savings as sellers clear out stock. But it’s rough out there. I do this for a living and it can be hard!”

“Maximizing value through limiting memory and storage is huge at the moment, with costs as high as they are,” Martindale says.

So ask yourself: How many games are you planning to keep on your laptop at the same time? (And if this will be your only laptop, how many photos, videos, work projects, etc.?) If you like having a plethora of preinstalled Steam games to pick from for any gaming session, you might need to shoot high: 1TB or more, which should give you plenty of space for a few heavy hitters (my Baldur’s Gate 3 installation sits at nearly 150GB, with Diablo 4 pushing up to 160GB and World of Warcraft at a whopping 213GB) and plenty of smaller friends (like the ever-charming Satisfactory at a mere 30GB, or Timberborn, which only eats up 2GB of space).

If you only really play one or two big games and a handful of smaller titles, you might be able to get away with 512GB. You’ll want to save around 10 to 15 percent free for your operating system to use, which is already going to feel tight, but it’s doable if it helps a more powerful laptop fit your budget better.

Display: 16 inches, OLED, 2560-by-1600 pixels | Processor: Intel Core Ultra 9 Processor 386H or AMD Ryzen AI 9 365 | Graphics: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060, 5070, 5070 Ti (up to 140W), 5080 (up to 165W), or 5090 (up to 165W) | Memory: 16- to 64-gigabytes; Storage | 1TB or 2TB; Ports: 3x USB 3.2 (Type-A), 1x Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C), 1X Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C), 1x microSD, 1x HDMI 2.1

Typically dubbed the “MacBook of gaming” by reviewers and gamers alike, Razer’s Blade 16 stands in a league of its own. It’s an expensive laptop as you start upgrading its parts from its base configuration, no question there, but the premium you pay is reflected in this system’s performance and prettiness. Unlike many souped-up gaming laptops, which can push double digits of weight, the Razer Blade 16 weighs just 4.7 pounds and sits at 14.9-mm thin when closed. That’s just two millimeters chubbier than a 16-inch MacBook Pro (and identical in weight), which means you shouldn’t have any issue lugging it around with you as a daily driver and gaming-desktop alternative.

The basic $2,400 configuration of the laptop (which you need to buy direct from Razer) gets you an AMD Ryzen AI 9 365 CPU paired with a Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 GPU, accompanied by a full terabyte of storage and 16GB of memory. That, plus effective thermal management means you should be able to get north of 60 frames per second on the higher settings of today’s most graphically intense titles. If you turn on the GPU’s DLSS image enhancement, you’ll likely see triple-digit frame rates, depending on the specific mode you use.

Though costlier, bumping up to Razer’s middle-of-the-road configuration puts you in the sweet spot. For an extra $1,100, you get Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 32GB of memory, and a Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU. You get a GPU that will allow you to turn on ray-tracing and max out your graphics settings while maintaining smooth, consistent gameplay — and a system that’s much stronger for multitasking, perfect for those managing streaming setups or encoding gameplay videos, or just plain power users who want a high-performance all-around machine. Simply put, you’ll be able to unlock more gorgeousness, and your investment will be more futureproofed.

The high-end version of the Blade 16, with a Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 GPU and 2TB of storage, costs nearly $5,000. While that looks like “the ultimate gaming setup” on paper, we don’t think it’s worth it. That’s high-end desktop PC money, and at that point it’s better to put the cash toward a laptop with a bigger screen (like the Razer Blade 18) if you really need to keep your gaming rig portable.

The Razer Blade 16 comes with a gorgeous 2,560-by-1,600-pixel OLED display that’s certified for VESA DisplayHDR TrueBlack 1000. It has excellent color accuracy out of the box, and its vivid colors and rich contrasts will make games like Cyberpunk 2077 look as good as their dystopian futures possibly could — a perfect pairing with the laptop’s incredible performance, so you’ll have great frame rates and a lovely picture to look at. The laptop’s glossy screen picks up reflections, however, so you may want to dim the lights in your gamer den for the best experience.

The laptop’s RGB keyboard lighting gives you that extra gamer aesthetic, and you can make it as wild or as subdued as you want via Razer’s Synapse app. It’s especially fun when one’s games can link directly to the app and change the keyboard’s colors, though I wish some of the effects were more interesting than just a simple static color (cough World of Warcraft cough). That’s Blizzard’s fault, though, not Razer’s, and you can DIY your own color setup and link it to a specific game, should you find the automatic results lacking.

If you need more storage, you can add an extra M.2 SSD into the Razer Blade 16 if you happen to have one lying around (that you haven’t put on eBay yet, that is). Otherwise, you have ample room to connect external storage and other devices, thanks to three USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports that join one Thunderbolt 5 port, one Thunderbolt 4 port, an SD card reader, one HDMI 2.1 port, and a 3.5-mm audio jack.

Display: 18 inches, OLED, Dual UHD+ 240 Hz / FHD+ 440 Hz | Processor: Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus or 275HX Plus| Graphics: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti (up to 140W), 5080 (up to 175W), or 5090 (up to 175W) | Memory: 32- to 128-gigabytes; Storage | 1TB or 2TB; Ports: 3x USB 3.2 (Type-A), 1x Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C), 1X Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C), 1x SD Card Reader, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 2.5-Gigabit Ethernet

If you just won the lottery, Razer’s Blade 18 is an even better (and bigger) version of its already premium Razer Blade 16. It costs even more than its sibling, and it’s less portable, but it’ll last you years to come — plenty of time to let your savings account heal. The larger screen gives you more immersion for your gameplay, and this is the only Razer laptop (as of when we wrote this) that offers access to the highest-performance processors you can get for your games and general use.

“We liked the Razer Blade 18 quite a bit, but it is very expensive, which makes me scream internally,” Biancuzzo says. “It’s got an RTX 5090, 32GB of RAM, and a giant 18-inch display that can go into two modes (3840-by-2400 at 240Hz or 1920-by-1200 at 440Hz). It also has TONS of ports, so you’re covered if you have a lot of gaming peripherals. It’s about as souped up as you can get.”

Biancuzzo looked at the highest-end Blade 18, though we recommend the stock trim, equipped with an Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti GPU. At that price, another big upgrade over the Razer Blade 16 is an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX processor, which you can bump up to the chart-topping Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX for an extra $500. These are the best-of-the-best Intel chips you can get as of when we published this article, rivaled only by AMD’s Ryzen 9 9955HX (which isn’t an option on the Razer Blade 18).

These Arrow Lake-HX chips can spit out anywhere from 10 percent to nearly double the performance of the Razer Blade 16’s Panther Lake and Zen 5 options, depending on the benchmarks. You might not see a huge impact in your games, but you’ll see a big boost in your multitasking — useful if you’re doing a ton of Twitch streaming, rendering your latest raid videos for YouTube, looking up strats across a bunch of browser tabs, and trying to game at the same time. This also futureproofs you for even longer than you’d get with the powerful but not chart-topping Razer Blade 16.

If you want even more desktop-like performance, you can also upgrade the GPU to either an RTX 5080 or 5090 (the latter locks you into 2TB of storage as well, up from the laptop’s 1TB default option). But the price you’ll pay for a completely maxed-out Razer Blade 18 makes less sense if this laptop is going to spend a majority of its life on your (gamer) desk. At that point, you’re likely better off with a dedicated, souped-up desktop gaming PC.

Display: 15.3 inches, OLED, 2560-by-1600 pixels | Processor: AMD Ryzen 7 250 | Graphics: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 (up to 130W) | Memory: 16 gigabytes | Storage | 512GB | Ports: 2x USB-C (65-100W Power Delivery), 3x USB-A, HDMI 2.1, Ethernet port

“If I had the least amount of money and just want the best performance? I would get the Lenovo LOQ / Legion 5 (at a reasonable price), or an [Asus] TUF A16,” Bennet says.

Lenovo’s Legion 5a has one critical upgrade over those other less-expensive machines that makes a huge difference if you care about the visual quality of your games and movies: A beautiful 2,560-by-1,600 OLED display that’s certified for DisplayHDR True Black 1000. This gets you visual quality that’s closer to a high-end machine like the Razer Blade 16 than most “budget” gaming laptops, along with a GPU, memory, and storage that matches the Blade’s base configuration. (The CPU, however, is slower, which could impact your gameplay if your favorite titles are more processor dependent.)

Because the Legion 5a pairs its higher resolution display with a less-powerful Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 GPU, as with the Razer Blade 16 you’ll likely need to rely on software settings such as DLSS to hit triple-digit frame rates in graphically punishing titles if you’re looking to max out your graphics settings. But you’re much more likely to notice and enjoy the richer contrasts and gorgeous true blacks of an OLED display over a traditional IPS display, so we think the trade-off is worth it.

Display: 15.6 inches, IPS, 1920-by-1080 pixels | Processor: AMD Ryzen 7 250 | Graphics: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 (up to 115W) | Memory: 16 gigabytes | Storage | 512GB | Ports: 1x USB-C (65-100W Power Delivery), 3x USB-A, HDMI 2.1, Ethernet port

If you want to spend as little as possible and prioritize performance over image quality, Laurence wholeheartedly recommends Lenovo’s LOQ 15, which you can typically find for around $1,300, pricing unpredictability aside.

“For the price, you’re getting really good specs, and the 5060 is about 15 to 20 percent faster in games than the 5050 [that you’ll find in cheaper gaming laptops], so if you can stretch your budget to this one, I would,” Laurence says. “If I were buying a reasonable gaming laptop right now, the LOQ is for sure the one I’d get.”

The configuration you’re looking for is respectable for mid-tier gaming: an AMD Ryzen 7 250 CPU; a Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 GPU; 16GB of memory; and a 15.3-inch, 1,200p display. You’ll run into plenty of configurations of this 15.3-inch laptop across various retailers, and the specs may differ slightly (a 1,080p display instead of 1,200p, for example). Make sure you’re selecting the right one if you’re shopping around.

As Bennet puts it: “An RTX 5060 is the minimum, and again, perfectly fine for 99 percent of people if you’re willing to play at 1,080/1,200p.”

entry.title: What Allison Williams Can’t Live Without
entry.summary: “If you have leaves with those colors, you’re going to end up in my house. But I’ll take really good care of you, I promise.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. We asked Allison Williams — who recently partnered with Dupixent — about the dual-fabric pillowcase, online plant service, and pretty packing cubes she can’t live without.

As you get older, your sleep quality ends up being one of the biggest factors in your life. Another thing that I love is the Ozlo Sleepbuds. It’s a little bit more of a splurge. Sometimes I like to fall asleep listening to an audiobook or something. This knows when you fall asleep, and then it switches to white noise, which is great. Also, it can make an alarm go off only in your earbuds, so you don’t have to wake up your partner or anyone else sleeping around you. This must mean that I’m truly an adult now, because I’ve started waking up early to go through my inbox and texts before my son and husband are awake. So, when my alarm goes off at like 5 a.m., I’m not also waking up my husband and son. That would be a very grumpy household. I’ve become very reliant on these.

I was always a morning hair washer, but I have become an evening hair washer because of a product that I found in New Zealand. It’s a silk pillowcase on one side and a towel material with waterproof backing on the other. This lets me sleep with wet hair without worrying that it’s going to destroy my pillow or that my hair stays super-wet while I’m asleep. It is a game changer.

I just added this brand-new smart ring product called the Pebble Index into my ecosystem. I read about it last year and was like, This is exactly what I need. This is what my brain needs to function at the level of other people’s brains. It’s supersimple but supereffective. It looks like the Oura Ring, except it has a button. You push it, you talk into the microphone, and you say something like, “Remind me in 20 minutes to take the pizza out of the oven,” and then it sends the reminder to your phone. That’s the only functionality. It can also listen to you brainstorm something or whatever, but that’s my use case for it. With that, I’ve actually been able to liberate myself from being tied to my phone. That sense of like, If I don’t write this down, it’ll be gone forever, is not an issue anymore. If I suddenly remember something I have to do while I’m driving or sitting at a dinner, this allows me to stay where I am rather than pulling out my phone and taking me out of the moment. I’m not wearing it today because I have these fancy, beautiful rings on, but I keep pushing this as if it’s the Pebble Ring, but it’s not. It’s already become a reflex.

I’ve posted about this on my Instagram, and I know you guys posted about it, but I wear a fanny pack all day, every day. Everything in there, I clearly can’t live without because it’s always attached to my body. It’s not on me, which makes me feel a little weird, but it is in my eyesight. It’s about eight feet from me. It’s basically all the same stuff in there as the post. Everything is super-consistent.

I have so many favorite snacks. When I find something I like, I go hard. I’m obsessed with these blondies by Bella’s Baked Goods; gluten-free Oreos are delicious. I love a fridge cig Diet Coke every once in a while. My ultimate snack food, though, is popcorn. And the version of it that I love the most — unfortunately for my health, because who knows what’s in it — is the Movie Theater Butter microwave-popcorn bags. That’s the GOAT in my book. It’s the one that I absolutely love.

Something I’ve discovered lately because they advertised on our podcast is Nuuly. I am obsessed. I don’t really shop for my personal life, because I know what sizes are like and I hate going to try on clothes. Nuuly cuts that corner. Also, for a short-attention-span clothing person, it’s perfect. You have something for a month, and then you send it back and get new stuff.

I used to only buy plants in person. It was like a chemistry thing. Like, if I saw a plant across the nursery, I was like, “You’re mine, I have to have you.” I recently discovered the Sill, though, and it gets me. I get emails from them that are like, “Look at this plant. Isn’t she pretty? She’s unusual.” And I end up buying it. I have — I’m not going to say the number, but it’s over 50 houseplants. I’m a sucker for a philodendron. A purple hue or a red hue just looks exotic to me. If you have leaves with those colors, you’re going to end up in my house. But I’ll take really good care of you, I promise.

Travel-wise, I’m a big packing-cube girl. I don’t know how I used to pack a chaos of clothes loose in a suitcase. It breaks my brain. Now, everything has to be in a packing cube; it doesn’t make sense to me otherwise. I love the Paravel ones. They’re so pretty. I have both the compression ones and non-compression normal ones. I use them depending on how intensely I’m trying to pack clothes into the suitcase. It’s like, Do I really need to squish all this stuff in here, or does it just look cute and fit perfectly? It’s almost never the second one, by the way. I’m an overpacker like crazy.

My mom got me wearing compression socks on flights in my mid-20s. She was like, “Listen, baby aspirin and compression socks. We’re not fucking around. You got to walk up and down the aisle. You got to move your body.” She was absolutely right, and I’m really glad that she got me in that habit. Then when all my friends were pregnant and having to start wearing compression socks, I was like, “Oh, I’ve been here. I’ve been wearing them. Let me tell you.” I have a vast variety of them, so that’s a necessity. No DVT here.

I lived my whole life with eczema on a level that I just tolerated. I had tried prescription topicals, but I still had flare-ups and lots of itching. Maybe because it was always in the same place (my calves) and somewhat predictable, that it was my normal. Then, it spread to my scalp. That triggered me to talk to my dermatologist and that’s when she told me about Dupixent. It’s had a specific and macro impact on me. On a macro level, the act of experiencing something for so long, and then deciding to do something about it is a revolutionary thing for me. Once it cleared up, I realized I have been letting it dictate what I wear on the bottom half of my body. Whether I wore shorts or pants was kind of determined by not just the temperature outside but often what my legs looked like. I had to wear gloves to sleep when I was little to try to stop myself from itching. It was definitely disruptive, but I thought it wasn’t something treatable when the prescription topicals weren’t working. Obviously, everybody is different, and people should talk to their own doctors to see if it’s right for them. But I just want to make the point that if you’re experiencing something daily that is uncomfortable, it’s possible you do not have to tolerate it. For people who have tried and failed with prescription topicals, and who have moderate-to-severe eczema, this is something that might work for you. I was part of that group.

entry.title: Everyone’s Showing Off Their Wired Headphones
entry.summary: I tested six pairs.
entry.content:
Save for prudent politicians and the frugal forgetful, it seemed that wired earbuds had gone extinct when Apple released the AirPods Pro. They had the benefits of noise cancellation and no fussy cords — and other than avoiding the expensive price, there really was no benefit to staying loyal to wired headphones. Despite all odds, though, wired buds are back. In recent months, they’ve popped up in photo dumps from Hailey Bieber and Kylie Jenner and are the common denominator among the gaggles of teens I see around the city. Most recently, I’ve noticed an influx of what I’d call fashion earbuds — colorful, chrome, and even embroidered pairs by everyone from Skullcandy and Sony to new (to me) brands, such as Chroma and Posh Tech. I’ve been using them to listen to podcasts and music and act as my speaker on FaceTime calls — all while styling them to match my outfits. My thoughts on every colorful pair I could find below.

Last year, I struggled to find a surprising and delightful Secret Santa gift under $25, but I think I’ll be gifting these to everyone this December. Compared to many of the other earbuds I tried, which have colorful cords, these take plain old white earbuds and dress them up with hand-wrapped embroidered thread that reminds me of the friendship bracelets I made as a tween. I’ve noticed that like any beloved friendship bracelet, the thread will fray with time and consistent use, but it doesn’t worsen the sound quality, which is solid for a pair of wired buds. I appreciate that the thread also adds some bulk and stiffness to the wires themselves, which prevents them from getting as tangled as your average wired headphones. There are a few color options available, but I’m into the light-pink version that would pair nicely with the pink Lululemon wristlet all the teens carry around.

These Sony earbuds are a happy medium between sound quality and color options. I’ve been using the blue ones, which pair nicely with my favorite navy-blue cardigan and add a subtle pop of blue to otherwise neutral outfits. There are also pink and black versions. The headphones are complete with thoughtful details, including protective casing where the cord meets the USB-C plug to prevent the cord from snapping or fraying. There’s also a fully functional control center and microphone on the left cord that allows you to adjust the volume, pause the music, and skip songs. As someone who’s always worried about my earbuds falling out, I appreciate that these come with three ear-tip sizes — the medium is perfect for me.

Chroma gave the Apple EarPods silhouette the chrome treatment, and I think the silver version would pair nicely with the wavy phone case that’s a staple in our gift guide for girlfriends. But if you’d like to match your headphones to your gold jewelry or find some buds that are your favorite color (should it be pink or blue), there are chrome versions for you, too. These are the least durable of the headphones I tried; the cord tangles easily and creases at friction points, like the edge of the control center and the base of the USB-C port. The chrome cover for the port also occasionally comes loose when I pull it out. But if you’re using these more for their looks than for prime engineering and sound quality, that shouldn’t be a problem. The fact that you can customize the port — there’s USB-C, Lightning, 3.5-mm. — is a nice plus, too.

I find it hard to resist a pop of red. I travel with a poppy-red suitcase, carry around a cherry-red wallet, and save my true red Le Bon Shoppe socks for the most special of occasions. These fire-engine-red headphones are the perfect addition to my collection, but there’s also a black version should the stereotypical New York uniform be more your style. They cost more than the aforementioned Le Bon Shoppe socks, but they’re less expensive than your average pair of wired earbuds, so I don’t feel the need to be as precious with them. Skullcandy didn’t cut corners — there’s a control center with basic capabilities (adjusting the volume, pausing the music, and skipping songs), and there are three ear tips to optimize the fit. They make for a surprising accessory for office attire and Saturday stroll outfits, and the sound quality is comparable to several of the other pairs I tried despite the cheaper price.

Unless purple is your favorite color, I’d skip this pair, which is available only in a very Olivia Rodrigo Sour shade. The headphones themselves are great quality — there’s no tinniness in the sound, and the three ear-tip options allow for an optimal, fuss-free fit. However, as someone who appreciates using the on-wire remote to control volume rather than getting sucked back into my phone, I couldn’t get past the limited capabilities on this one. The control center is just a microphone that can pause and skip — no volume control. At that point, why add one at all?

Unless you’re an avid gymgoer, you probably don’t need these headphones, which have two fits: in-ear and over the ear, the latter of which provides even more security should you be worried about your earbuds falling out during a run or other workout. The headphones themselves are some of the most comfortable to wear — they have three ear-tip sizes and a bulkier, ear-sealing base that gives the illusion of noise cancellation even though these buds don’t have that capability. The cord itself is also sturdier than most, making the wires less tangly than some of the others I tried (notably, the Chroma and Sony buds). There’s even extra support where the cord meets the USB-C port, which is often where I see signs of wear first. I also appreciate that the buds are magnetic, so they stick to each other rather than contributing to a tangled mess. Only the black and navy-blue versions are available now, but I spotted a gross green and purple version in the spec sheet that I hope JBL will restock.

entry.title: A Stirrup Skeptic’s Hunt for Stirrups
entry.summary: “Depending on one’s height and the amount of stretch in the pants, I envisioned a tug-of-war between the waist and the feet.”
entry.content:
Back in the ’80s, stirrup pants were the polished, sportswear-esque alternative to gym clothes. Still basically leggings, they had a hint of the equestrian to them — and unlike with standard leggings, something about that extra strap of fabric underfoot telegraphed sophistication. As early as third grade I wanted a pair of my own, but I wore a daily school uniform and my judicious mother deemed them a frivolous purchase. Lately, though, stirrup pants are back on my mind.

Stirrups were all over the runways this past season in various forms, from suiting-inspired styles to classic athletic pants (see Stella McCartney, Jil Sander, Tibi), and I’ve seen them plenty off the runway, too. I’ve spotted them in workout classes, on the subway during the workday rush hour, and on celebrities like Amal Clooney and Beyoncé. Still, I was skeptical about how flattering they could be on taller bodies like mine. Depending on one’s height and the amount of stretch in the pants, I envisioned a tug-of-war between the waist and the feet. I’m five-foot-ten, so I set out to see for myself.

I gravitated toward these stirrup leggings for their seam running down the front of the leg. I think that always makes a pant look more polished and considered, even athletic styles. Alas, these weren’t long enough to get up over my hips, but they’d make a terrific and versatile entry-level pair of stirrup pants for someone just a few inches shorter.

Aside from the length issues I had with these, I’m just not sure I could have pulled off their slick faux-leather look. Although I really did love the buttery-soft, smooth texture and how closely they resembled actual leather.

Similar to the above style by Zara, these also have a piped seam down the front. Of all the pairs I tried, they were the most lightweight and probably the softest, which makes them a good piece for traveling light and even wearing en route (so much more stylish than airplane sweatpants).

Like the neoprene option I tried from Commando, these had a great body-contouring quality, but they were a little too densely knit for my liking. To me, the best pants and leggings are the ones you forget you’re wearing. I did appreciate the high-rise waist, though, which made for smoother lines all-around.

Leset’s stirrup pants have been popular among several girlfriends with whom I share shopping notes, so I was excited to take them for a spin. The fabric is a viscose-based stretch ponte (a densely knit, more substantial cousin to jersey) that’s conforming and pretty comfortable once you’ve got these fully on, but you have to work for it. Like a good pair of compression stockings, I really had to tug to get these all the way up my legs.

I liked their deep brown shade and matched them with a taupe suede button-down from Arma and brown zebra-print d’Orsay flats by J.Crew from forever ago. I’d also style them with dressy open-backed heels or even a pair of Birkenstock mules in a matching taupe for a casual day of be-bopping around town.

I felt like an off-duty dancer in these sheer tights, which bore more of a full open foot than a stirrup, leaving mostly just my toes exposed (kind of like leg warmers when they’re pulled over the foot). As far as tights go, these are a medium on the opacity scale — still too sheer to wear as pants alone, so I wore mine with cut-off shorts, a T-shirt, and mesh mary-janes. I loved them. However, they didn’t make the winners’ circle on the technicality that their sheerness disqualifies them from the “leggings” category. Despite their description online, these are 100 percent tights in my book.

Similar to the sheer H&M leggings I tried on, this heathered-gray pair by Zara feel more like stockings to me than advertised. Made from an acrylic-poly blend, they’re easy to get on and seem like they’d be a really cozy option for keeping my legs warm in the winter, except I already have an overabundance of (fully closed-toe) tights that do the same thing.

I laughed when I first held these Commando leggings up wondering how far I’d actually manage to yank them up my legs — and if I’d lose a fingernail in the process. But wow do they stretch, and with remarkable ease considering the compressing qualities of the neoprene.

As far as leggings go, I found them the most supportive and flattering thanks to the weight of the material. You feel really “held in,” but not uncomfortably. I wore these with an Adidas windbreaker and Birkenstock sandals for a post–hot yoga look and loved how sleek and long my legs seemed in them.

Without question, the Frankie Shop’s ribbed knit leggings were the most comfortable of the options I tried on — and they made me genuinely excited to wear them. While most of the other candidates comprised synthetics or cotton blends for stretch, these are entirely made from merino wool, and have the same pull-on ease as a beloved ribbed turtleneck. That said, they’re definitely better-suited for “sweater weather,” which is fine in my book — those days are coming, and these pants check a lot of boxes in terms of dressing options. I’d wear them for weekend errands as a stylish alternative to sweatpants, maybe with an oversize chunky sweater. But they’d also work with a slim knit top or T-shirt, tucked in and layered with a blazer, for a dressier look.

Yes, these are a lot pricier than the other pairs I tried, but I loved them for the unique sporty aesthetic of their jogger-style silhouette and the smart adjustable stirrups, which allowed them to be worn over heeled shoes or boots. Also, I appreciate anything with pockets.

From the waist, these seem like your typical pair of athletic pants, thick waistband and all, so I paired them with a relaxed-fitting white T-shirt, tucked in. There’s something about that superfluous stirrup detail that makes you look twice, but it’s refreshing when a garment reminds you that you can wear things simply because they look interesting and different, and sometimes that’s enough — no radical function required.

entry.title: The 30 Best Things Strategist Staffers Bought in October
entry.summary: “I rarely buy new everyday sneakers, but as soon as I saw these, I knew they were what I wanted in a fall pair.”
entry.content:
Obviously, Strategist staffers are excellent shoppers — that’s why you’re visiting the site right now. So once a month, we highlight the things we’ve been buying for ourselves. You’ll notice it’s both a blessing and a curse to be a Strategist editor: We’re picky, but sometimes we just have to get on with it. (It’s online-shopping expertise meets IRL needs.) Below, what we bought in October.

I’ve been counting down the days until I’m next at an Erewhon, where I first discovered these gummies, so I can buy a dozen more packs. In the growing arena of gummy candies that aren’t really gummy candies or candy that’s good for you, these are the best-tasting ones I’ve tried (SmartSweets who?). Soft, pillowy, and chewy, they’re never hard or overly dense like other contenders I’ve had. They truly taste like gummy candies — sweet and just the right amount of tangy — which makes them hard to put down. Plus, how can you beat getting 68 percent of your daily fiber value at under 100 calories a pack?

I suppose I’m always on the prowl for the next best thing hair-wise, and I discovered this on a whim. It’s everything I wanted the Color Wow spray to be (which I tried years ago and discovered was a massive flop). It’s essentially the only heat protectant I’ve been using on my hair for weeks now and I’ve never gotten more compliments on my blowouts. One of my friends even thought I’d gotten a Brazilian blowout. Mist this through wet hair and then blow-dry with tension. My hair is smoother than usual after fewer passes than I usually have to do per section, and it’s plenty shiny after straightening the roots too. Plus it keeps hair sleek for days on end, even after a light misting.

I like cute Halloween decorations (no blood, gore, or ghouls in my house). To supplement my collection of bats, black cats, and friendly ghosts, I bought this spiderweb to drape over the fireplace. It’s quite effective for being so simple. It also feels pretty nice for being under $10, and I hope to use it for numerous Halloweens to come.

My second-grader loves wearing striped shirts, and some of his favorites come from Hanna Andersson. I stocked up on a couple during a sale, including this version that I would wear myself. He also loves the brand’s ringer shirts, but I forgot to add to cart this time.

I’ve been wanting a really good soup bowl for a while now, and while East Fork’s aptly named Soup Bowl would be my top choice, I wasn’t ready to spend quite so much. My chance to finally have my desired bowl (at my desired price) came earlier this month at East Fork’s Seconds sale in Asheville. While I hadn’t anticipated having to stand on line in the rain to secure my bowls, now that I’ve brought them home, I think they were well worth the trouble. The bowls are just the right level of deep and wide for eating soup — all my other bowls are either too deep and narrow or too wide and shallow — and eating out of them just feels extra homey and cozy.

I rarely buy new everyday sneakers, but as soon as I saw these, I knew they were what I wanted in a fall pair. I love the slim nylon shape — it is not quite a sneakerina but isn’t bulky — and the burgundy color looks nice with jeans and black pants. I also love that they have little gum-sole cleats on the bottom — not that I need cleats for walking around the city, but the sole does add some texture and maybe (maybe?) feels slightly grippier on the subway stairs.

We are expecting a baby next month (!) and have spent the past few weeks getting our apartment ready. Most of our baby-related shopping has been very practical — stroller bunting, a carrier, first-aid kit, etc. — but I was so charmed by this elephant that I couldn’t resist.

While killing time before seeing a movie on the Lower East Side, I fell in love with the charm bar at the Susan Alexandra storefront. I had somehow never been before and was surprised by the number of charm and necklace options on offer. I’m usually not big on impulse purchases, but I bought one of the single-charm premade necklaces the company sells in store. I got the star to replace my other everyday star necklace that has seen better days. (I will be back for a multi-charm statement necklace in the future, though …)

I’m due in March with my first child, so Hanna Andersson’s very good fall sale inspired me to buy my first batch of baby clothes. My husband and I are big Peanuts and Snoopy fans, so we had to grab these winter and Halloween sleepers for the holidays next year. (Doesn’t hurt to plan ahead, right?)

I spent last weekend slinging biscuits at the Yeshi Sunday Market and ended up using most of our profits to buy things available there. I bought three items: a version of these candlestick holders from Yam; a tub of shea butter from Hanahana, a brand I’ve been using since 2020; and a bag charm from Louna Ceramics.

This month, I made it my goal to better organize the top of my dresser, which had become a dumping ground for necklaces, stray beauty products, and probably a few too many hair brushes. I tackled the jewelry problem with this spacious box that still has some empty spots for pieces to come. As for the beauty products, I got a three-tiered organizer that spins.

I have been recovering from a back injury and struggling to carry my bags while traveling alone. I’ve been debating solving my problem with this under-the-seat rolling bag that Sally Jessy Raphael recommended on our site last year, and after regretting my personal-item choices one too many times, I decided it was worth it. If I’m also checking a bag, I roll around my additional personal item on top of this one (in that case, it acts as a carry-on to hold more travel essentials). I imagine after my back heals, I’ll still use it, as it takes all the schlepping out of traveling. Perhaps the kids using the rolling backpacks are wise beyond their years.

A boring but very useful buy. The angled blades and grippy handle make trimming my cats’ nails a little less of a chore.

I’ve also been buying a lot of kitchen staples, and this is one of our best chef’s knives. It’s great quality for the price, and as noted in our Best in Class guide, it’s deceptively lightweight without feeling flimsy. I don’t have a dishwasher, and hand-washing has been fairly simple.

I’ve made it a point this fall to be on top of my supplements, and this has changed the game. I can fit weeks’ worth of multivitamins, vitamin D, fish oil, and probiotics into this sippy cup–esque organizer and simply twist and dispense each pill. I can leave it out on my kitchen counter, and it’s much more travel friendly than a pill case. While it’s slightly bulky, I’m able to add ibuprofen, allergy pills, and one or two over-the-counter medicines I’d usually bring bottles of in case of emergency, so it ultimately cuts down on space.

I usually associate the brand Rat Boi with its delicate pointelle tanks, but the latest fall collection included some very good tees. I ended up going with this striped one, and it’s quickly become a piece I’ve reached for repeatedly. It’s soft yet structured, oversize but not billowy on my five-foot-one frame, and the jewel tones are the perfect pop of color for my autumn wardrobe.

This month, I finally decided to divest from my iPhone camera (which is cracked anyway). They just make everyone look terrible. I’m not a techy person, but my cousin has this little Canon point-and-shoot that she used to take some great photos of me last summer, so that was good enough for me. So far, it’s been super easy to use. I’ve even taken it out for a reporting story I’m working on that requires photography, and I’m really impressed with the results. This might be common knowledge, but I learned it the hard way (again, not a tech person), that you do need to purchase a memory card separately for this camera, so make sure to budget for that accordingly.

October was a big month for me: A few days before I started working at the Strategist, I moved to a bigger apartment. One of my first crucial buys for the new place was a kitchen trash and recycling setup that didn’t live under the sink. While I was tempted by the Amazon Prime Day discounts on the sleek Caraway trash cans that look too pretty for the things I’d put in them, I still couldn’t stomach spending more than $200 on a trash can. Plus I face the same problem with its matching recycling bins that senior writer Emma Wartzman does — my boyfriend needs a much bigger bin for his Diet Coke habit. I ultimately chose Songmics’ dual-compartment eight-gallon bins for recycling and a 13-gallon trash can with a similar profile, which cost me about $300 less than Caraway’s pair. I only wish that the trash can came in the dual-compartment bins’ chic greenish-gray color that looks like it could be part of Caraway’s collection.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has finally delivered a camera I trust enough to leave my dedicated camera at home — no small accomplishment since I’m a new dad who’s taking many times more photos than I have at any other point in my life. Its wider maximum aperture provides better low-light performance for capturing a squirmy baby under lamp light, and the fact that it adjusts mechanically (like in a real camera lens) lets me achieve artfully blurred backgrounds without relying on computer-generated portrait effects. But the biggest upgrade is actually in the camera app, which finally offers quick-access full manual controls over all the most important settings (like aperture, white balance, and shutter speed). I especially appreciate being able to enter RAW shooting mode in just a few taps to disable all the post-capture processing tricks that occasionally lead to unnatural-looking images. If I was in a stage of life where taking photos was less important, I’d still be carrying the lighter iPhone Air, but the 18 Pro’s camera is just so much better that I’m happy to carry the extra weight.

As a big fan of the original Sonos Ace, I’m happy to report that the new Ace Ultra is just as comfortable as the original (I wore it on back-to-back cross-country flights with no pain or tingling in my ears or scalp) and even better in every other regard. Whereas the original Ace was a simple Bluetooth headphone with some Sonos compatibility, the Ultras have built-in Wi-Fi for better integration with the rest of the Sonos system. This lets you play the same song or podcast on the headphones and speakers at the same time without any syncing issues. This is particularly handy if you have a Sonos soundbar and want to watch TV without disturbing sleeping members of your household — although the original Ace could also do this via Bluetooth. Personally, I had no issues with the original’s limitations in this regard (my headphone listening rarely intersects with my speaker listening), but I have been appreciating the Ultra’s improved noise cancelling while working from the same small apartment as a fussy infant who’s fighting sleep. I wouldn’t recommend rushing to upgrade if you already have the original Ace or a comparable set of noise canceling headphones from Sony, Bose, or Apple. But if you don’t have headphones you love and are all in on Sonos’s speakers, the Ultras are worth the premium over the originals.

I lost my nice sunglasses after a two-year run — really not bad for me. I didn’t want to spend a fortune on a replacement pair because, well, I’m likely to lose them again. I popped into Warby Parker this past weekend, which historically has been hit-or-miss for me. But luckily, I found a pair I really like. They had to get shipped, so they’re arriving tomorrow, and I’m excited to not be squinting every time I go outside.

I recently had a fantastic meal at King (it really does keep hitting), so it felt fateful when I found a $10 copy of The King Cookbook, which came out last year, at a used bookstore in Prospect Heights the other day. After flipping through and looking at the recipes, I determined I would actually use it (rare for a restaurant cookbook).

While researching natural-fiber base layers for a Strategist Hunt, I came across Little Spruce Organics, a shop in Colorado that is the sole United States stockist for a ton of European brands. (Also lots of cute kid stuff, like this wool-and-silk shirt and this baby sweater.) I ordered four things immediately; my two favorites were this organic cotton shirt from Living Crafts and the hemp socks below. The shirt is truly perfect — soft and smooth and garment-dyed using a method that draws attention to small design details.

I also love these cotton-hemp socks — lightweight and airy, special but not fussy. They don’t have any elastic, so they stretch out a bit by the end of the day but shrink back down after washing.

I recently got third lobe piercings at Catbird, but unfortunately, during the healing process, my ears were feeling somewhat swollen and irritated due to the fact that I tempted fate and continued to sleep on my side. (I know, I know — I just can’t fall asleep on my back!) The original studs were a little pokey, so I swapped them out for these low-profile threader earrings from Theirs, whose unisex jewelry designs I’ve loved and written about before. They are the perfect length, not overly long or dangly; style seamlessly with my other earrings; and feel extremely comfortable to sleep in. I basically wore them 24/7 for weeks on end, but I recently lost one. (I really need to be more careful while changing for dance class.) Thankfully, the brand sells them in singles, so I speedily purchased a replacement.

During a trip to Asheville earlier this month, I picked up this book of old-fashioned pumpkin recipes at the Southern Highland Craft Guild, an Appalachian folk-art museum. It’s got several recipes for pumpkin pies, plus breads, cookies, cakes, puddings, ice cream, and more. I’ve been perusing in search of inspiration for this year’s Thanksgiving dessert.

I didn’t even know that vacuum steamers existed before reading Schwartz’s review of them, but as soon as I got to their description of the Rowenta, I knew it was the one for me.

I’m always willing to try a promising-sounding new-to-me pen, especially one that’s so cheap.

entry.title: I’ve Tested More Than 20 Robot Vacuums. These Are the Best.
entry.summary: They’ll keep hard floors and carpets free of debris.
entry.content:
Robot vacuums can clean up your house or apartment, even when you’re not at home — no effort necessary on your part, unless you count pushing a button (and since they can work on a schedule, you don’t really even need to do that).

Using motion sensors, lasers, a camera, or some combination of the three, the latest robot vacuums can navigate your household and clean thoroughly without running into furniture or falling down the stairs. Most create maps to remember the layout of your home, some can recognize stray objects like toys and socks, while others use more basic systems that don’t store any data about your home. As with regular vacuums, these robots can get quite noisy while working, so you probably shouldn’t schedule them to run any time you wouldn’t vacuum by hand. And if you’re particularly sensitive to noise, be sure you are in another room or away from home when it’s cleaning (or have a good pair of noise-canceling headphones).

You can find many robot vacuum brands offering models with similar-sounding specs, but this is a category in which it’s best to stick to reputable makers. I focused on vacuums from Eufy, Roborock, Dyson, Ecovacs, Matic, and Narwal, as they’re some of the most established brands in the space and make an array of vacuums that suit the needs of both small and large homes.

To find the best robot vacuum for every type of home and lifestyle, I tested more than 20 robot vacuums in my home, which I share with two other people and five dogs, on short-pile carpet, hardwood, and tile, assessing how well they clean, how effectively they navigated my home, and how much hands-on work they required.

If you’re looking for a robot vacuum for handling pet hair and messes, we have a separate guide for those, but just know that all our picks below are up to the task.

One final note: Earlier this year the FCC announced a ban on imported foreign-manufactured “advanced robotic devices,” which includes robot vacuums. While the future of robot vacuums remains uncertain as manufacturers adapt to the new terms, every robot vacuum we recommend has already been approved and will remain available despite the ban, which only applies to new models.

Updated on October 29, 2026
I’ve added the Narwal Flow 2 as our new best robot vacuum for deep-pile carpets. I’ve also removed the Eufy C10 as our best less-expensive robot vacuum, as it’s no longer available — I’ll be testing more budget-friendly options soon. Everything else is still available and the prices are up-to-date.

Although suction power is the primary metric flaunted by vacuum manufacturers, the vacuum’s brushes are just as important when it comes to picking up debris that’s deeply embedded in your tile and carpet. A good robot vacuum will have a brush (or multiple brushes) that can create enough agitation to break up particles that weaker vacuums might miss, like dried-up mud. Weak brushes will simply sweep over the top of your carpets and rugs, while a more thorough brush will dig deep into the fibers and kick up anything that’s stuck below the surface. Many robot vacuum cleaners even have side brushes that can help clear up corners and other tough-to-reach spots.

Better brushes don’t just make it easier to clean the floors, either; they make your vacuum last longer on each charge. The more work the brush does to scrape things off your surfaces, the less suction power (and energy) a vacuum has to use to completely remove it. A motor running at maximum will have enough suction power to yank things out of your carpet, but it may take longer to complete a cleaning job as it’ll have to recharge more often. Meanwhile, a vacuum with slightly weaker suction power but more effective brushes will clean up more debris and require fewer trips back to the charging station.

Although it’s true that suction power isn’t as important for the performance of a robot vacuum as the brushes it uses, it still matters. Since I first started working on this guide three years ago, robot vacuums have gotten more powerful, making them more effective at pulling dirt and hair out of carpets. Suction is commonly measured in Pascals (Pa) to indicate the amount of air pressure the vacuum is applying. Generally, the higher the pressure, the more suction power, and the better a vacuum will be at picking things out of carpets and rugs. But keep in mind that that number shows how much it’s capable of applying at maximum settings, which you have to enable.

If a vacuum cleaner doesn’t have enough juice to clean your entire home on a single charge, it will need to run back to its base station to replenish itself before finishing the job. Most robot vacuums have batteries capable of cleaning long enough to cover a decent-size home, but larger homes may require multiple charges. Some robot vacuum cleaners have software that calculates how much juice a robot vac needs to complete the job and only charges enough to cover that and return to the base, which will help it get back to cleaning and wrap things up sooner.

Despite what the name implies, these gadgets should be judged as vacuums first and robots second. No software feature can make up for a subpar job picking up debris off your floors. Part of effectively replacing a manual cleaning system is being able to trust that your robot vacuum won’t miss any spots in its cleaning cycles, and that your floors will be at least as clean as if you’d done the job yourself.

Some robot vacuums accomplish this by creating a map of your home, complete with obstacle identification and no-go zones, so you can program it to only clean specific areas on a given day. More basic robot vacuums use an infrared sensor to identify obstacles and other objects to avoid, but fancier models take it a step further with a built-in camera you can use to pinpoint items that might only be there for one cleaning cycle, like a stray toy one of your kids left out. Some newer models create live updates of your home’s map and store it all locally, so nothing gets sent back to the company’s servers.

If you’re splurging on a robot vacuum, you want one that offers the most convenience possible. Given how small the robots themselves are, they typically have pretty small chambers for holding dirt and debris, so you’ll have to clean them out more often than you may be used to with a more traditional vacuum cleaner.

Some companies offer models that have self-emptying bases where the robot will dispose of all of the dirt once it’s finished a cleaning job (or its chamber is full and it needs to be emptied before resuming cleaning). They’re more expensive, but you’ll also spend less time clearing things out of your vacuum, and emptying the containers inside the base is easier than cleaning the robot itself. Fair warning, though: Those bases are often louder than the vacuums themselves. You may want to run it when no one is home, or just make sure you don’t schedule a cleaning during a work call.

Filtration is key to an effective vacuum cleaner. Without good filtration, you’ll end up with a lot of dust blown right back into the air and, ultimately, landing back on your floors to be cleaned up and tossed back out during your next cleaning cycle.

Most companies don’t list a ton of details about their filtration systems, but you should avoid any vacuum that doesn’t mention having filters at all. Usually, you can check by looking at the “What’s included in the box” section of the product listing.

Whatever robot you buy, it should last more than a few years: Even the cheapest options are still costly. The more parts you can replace on your own, the less likely you are to need to buy a whole new vacuum when things go wrong. In the best cases, you can replace everything from the brushes and filters to the wheels and batteries.

Robot vacuums with mopping capabilities have been around for quite a while now, but they’ve only gotten particularly good over the last couple years. Newer models have features like rotating mop pads (often two), hot-water cleaning built into the docks, and in some cases mopping pads that swivel out to reach corners and other spots that are tough to reach. Others come with a mopping brush that can self-clean as it’s mopping your floors, so it doesn’t have to return to a docking station repeatedly while cleaning.

While robots with mopping functions may not be as effective as a dedicated wet floor cleaner, they get about 90 percent of the way there, so you won’t notice unless you’re particular about the cleanliness of your floors. Of course, it’ll also depend on how dirty your floors tend to get and how frequently they require cleaning. Every robot I’ve tested has the ability to customize cleaning routines, so you can use light or heavy water settings as needed.

If you do opt for a vacuum-mop combo, you’ll have to use a cleaning solution to achieve maximum cleanliness. Many companies offer proprietary fluids that you dispense into the robot, but there are also third-party options available. Just be sure to get one that’s compatible with your robot, information you’ll usually be able to find on the front of the bottle. You can also use the robot’s mopping function with plain water, and even that does a decent job of keeping your floors clean.

Robot vacuums typically come with their own apps; while some also have integrations with smart assistants like Alexa, Google Home, and, in a few cases, Siri, you’ll probably find yourself sticking to the manufacturer’s app anyway. These smart home assistants do make triggering the robot’s core cleaning functions easy, you won’t be able to use them to fine-tune your settings, like adjusting the number of cleaning cycles or how much water your robot’s mopping function uses — you’ll have to do all that in the app.

If you have kids (or curious pets) in your house, you’ll want to ensure your robot has a child-lock feature. With this mode enabled, no one can trigger a cleaning job by pressing the robot’s on-device buttons. You’ll usually need to go to the app to enable this mode, but some robots also let you turn it on right from the device’s buttons.

Brushes: Single rubber brush | Suction power: 10,000 Pa | Battery run time: 150 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors | Disposal: Self-emptying base station | Filtration: Yes | Repairability: Replaceable brush, dustbins, filters, and disposal bags | Mopping: Yes | Voice assistant: Alexa, Google Home | Child lock: Yes

Roborock’s vacuums have earned spots in several iterations of this guide thanks to their excellent mapping software and ability to thoroughly suck up tons of dirt and gunk. That’s especially true of the Q7 M5+, which has high suction power and is packed with features to ensure it can successfully avoid obstacles and clean up all the tough-to-reach spots in your house. In a home with five dogs, this vacuum managed to pick up a week’s worth of dirt and hair without any issues.

The Q7’s software makes mapping your home a breeze. It took about half an hour to map my home, while some robots, like those from Ecovacs, took about 15 minutes longer. And even with a floor covered in pet toys and dog bowls, plus several tables and chairs, this robot never got stuck or required saving.

You can customize your robot’s cleaning cycles by setting it to clean only designated rooms, or set a specific zone inside a room for a quick cleaning job like a spill. I mostly rely on the 2-D map created by the vacuum, but there’s also a 3-D map you can view, which is handy for sending your vacuum to clean hard-to-reach spots like under your bed. The app lets you add your own boundaries within rooms and place furniture onto the map. You can also build custom routines that clean up rooms at specified times. To ensure you stay current on your robot’s maintenance, the app gives an estimate of how long each component — brushes, filters, etc. — will last before needing to be replaced.

For tough-to-clean floors, there’s a Turbo mode that increases the vacuum’s suction. That mode drains the battery faster and makes the vacuum louder, but it also works great and has kept my rugs clean from crumbs and other specks of dirt. The more suction power you use, the shorter the battery will last, but Roborock’s software allows the robot to go back and recharge without losing its place in the cleaning process.

Unlike previous picks for the best robot vacuum overall, the Q7 M5+ also functions as a mop. It’s not as good at mopping as more fully featured vacuum-mop combos like the Matic or Narwal Flow 2, but the feature is nice to have. The mopping pad doesn’t come installed, and the dock doesn’t have a mop-cleaning function, so you have to do it yourself (by hand or in the washing machine). Additionally, it can’t apply as much pressure as the Matic or Narwal, so it isn’t as effective at scrubbing floors. If you need a robot that can frequently mop your floors without needing you to do a weekly mopping job yourself, get the Matic.

The biggest omission in this robot is its lack of Siri integration. Other Roborock vacuums support it, so I wish it were included here.

Brushes: Single brush | Suction power: 3,200 Pa | Battery run time: 180 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors, camera | Disposal: Manually emptied bag with diaper salts | Filtration: Yes | Repairability: Replaceable water tank, brushes, HEPA bag, mopping pads | Mopping: Yes | Voice assistant: None | Child lock: Yes

In my three years of testing robot vacuum-mop combos, none has impressed me as quickly as Matic’s. Its charming design — sort of like a robotic turtle — is more fun to look at than the typical puck shape of other robot vacuums. The dock, which doesn’t have a dirty-water tank or dustbin, is quite small compared to other vacuum-mop combos such as the Narwhal. Instead, everything gets done on the robot itself.

Compared to other robot vacuums I’ve tested, its mapping is quite fast. Where many other robots tend to move slowly and take their time scanning each room, the Matic whizzed across the floor to create an equally accurate map in under 20 minutes.

Like its mapping process, cleaning is surprisingly quick. It managed to clean two bedrooms, plus a common area and one bathroom, in about 45 minutes. In all that time, it only got caught on one thing: A loose thread on my carpet that I had to clip with scissors to prevent the Matic from getting stuck on it again. Other than that, it managed to avoid stray cables and cords, and my floors are nice and shiny after every cleaning job.

That’s a result of Matic’s unique smarts. Most robot vacuums depend on the initial map it creates to navigate your home, which means they have to rely on the company’s servers for object recognition. Most of that data comes from customers, so it’s not the ideal route if you’re privacy conscious. The Matic, on the other hand, constantly updates its map based on what it sees; none of that data gets sent back to Matic. To ensure it gets all the dirtiest messes — juice spills, dropped cereal, stray pet food — the Matic can automatically tweak its settings based on what its cameras see.

It’s even great at getting to spots that other robot vacuums might miss. Thanks to its taller body, which gives the Matic’s cameras a higher placement than other robot vacuums, it can see more of your house. The company’s app allows you to get a live view of what the Matic sees, and if you can find a way to get to a spot that the robot is struggling with, you can tap “Go here” and help it find its way. That doesn’t happen often, as the Matic is quite good at navigating on its own, but when it does happen, it makes using a robot vacuum feel almost like playing a video game.

Another thing I love about this robot: It doesn’t get stinky like other vacuums can. A colleague once mentioned that they’d stopped using their robot vacuum because the dirty water tank is easy to forget about and smells absolutely horrible after sitting for more than a week. The Matic, which has a single HEPA bag that stores dirty water as well as dirt and debris it’s picked up, fights odors with diaper salts embedded in the bag. That way, you won’t have to plug your nose when you empty it, which should be every couple weeks.

The Matic does struggle with three things. First, its height prevents it from reaching places traditional puck-shaped vacuums can reach, like underneath the couch. Additionally, it can’t clean edges as well as those robots, so you may need to do some manual vacuuming or dusting near your baseboards. Finally, its suction power is notably weaker than that of vacuums like the Narwal Flow 2, making it less effective for deeper-pile rugs.

Brushes: Single brush | Suction power: 31,000 Pa | Battery run time: 210 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors, camera | Disposal method: Self-emptying base station for dirt and liquid | Filtration: Yes | Repairability: Replaceable brush, dust bin, filter, mopping pads | Mopping: Yes; hot-water cleaning | Voice assistant: Alexa, Siri | Child lock: Yes

If you have deep-pile carpets, you’ll need something with more suction power. Narwal’s Flow 2 is a powerful, efficient vacuum that does an excellent job at yanking out dirt and other nasty stuff that’s been caked into the fibers of your carpet. I tested this by pouring a handful of coffee grounds on my rug and having the Flow run a quick spot-cleaning job — barely anything was left behind for me to clean up by hand. That’s largely in part thanks to the Flow 2’s high suction power, which also works better for sucking pet hair out of rugs and carpets.

Like Roborock, Narwal makes setup and maintenance pretty straightforward. The robot will automatically start mapping your home after you finish connecting it to your network, and you can easily have it cleaning in about 30 minutes. While not on par with Matic’s, the Flow 2’s software is also quite smart: It’s able to detect stains and particularly messy areas so it can adjust its settings and ensure every mess gets cleaned accordingly. For instance, if it sees some dried-up soda you spilled earlier, the vacuum will go over the area repeatedly with its mopping pad to ensure that spot gets cleaned without having to go over your entire kitchen floor again.

Smarts aside, this is a darn good vacuum and mop. Its suction power is enough to yank all sorts of gunk out of rugs and carpet, and its mopping has been effective enough that I could confidently leave all my floor maintenance to this robot — it’s left my floors squeaky clean. And you can fine-tune the settings of the robot to clean your floors as thoroughly as you’d wish. It can vacuum and mop simultaneously or one after the other, up to three times, and you’re able to control how much suction and water the vacuum uses while cleaning.

Unlike the Matic, the Narwal has clean and dirty water tanks on its self-emptying dock, so maintenance is relatively hands off. After every cleaning job, the vacuum will return to its station and clean its mopping pads, leaving them as good as new. And while many robot vacuums feature docks that stick out among typical room décor, the Flow 2’s design is subtle enough as to not draw unwanted attention. It’s also quite slim and I was able to easily wedge it into a narrow space between a table and bookshelf with room to spare.
